div.head: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
div.p: PLEASANT PARAGRAPHS.
DON'T be afraid to speak well of yourself; there are plenty who are only too anxious to speak ill

:of you. "I READ so many cases of people being .buried alive. Is there no remedy for it?" "inc only remedy I know is for Parliament to pass a law: .compelling doctors to finish their work properly." " WERE you at the opera last night?" "Yes" " How did you like the tout enseinble?" ' " Not very well. I.thought that the orchestra gave us entirely too much toot as well as too Much cymbals." A JUROR asked to be excused on the ground of ,deafness. The judge asked the juryman if he had .heard the charge. "Yes, your Honour, but ni be hanged if I could make head or tail of it:" He was excused. • You may say what you will about pictures of iistonishment, but you just ought to see a frog try to jump into a pool of water that is frozen over. Be don't say much, and what he does say can't be relied upon. Atz Irish peasant being asked why he permitted 'his pig to take up its quarters with his family, -made an answer abounding with satirical naivette —" Why uqk? Doesn't the place afford every coh- venience that a pig can require ?" Visrron (in penitentiary)—" What brCeight pin to this place, my friend ? ' Convict=" Sneezing." Visitor—" Sneezing l" Convict—" Yis, sorr. It woke the gibtlemao up an' he nabbed mo. Haire • ye got a bit of tobbacey about ye, sem I" I'll ASTER-4' John; how is this? This litter must have arrived a week ago, and your have only knit • given it to me." Valet—" But, sir, it only Makes an appointment for to-morrow, and I did not think it neve:so:cry to hand it to you before." liosTvss—" What has become of Sandy Smith, who . stood so high in your class?" Alumnus— "Oh, he's taken orders SOME] time." Hostess.= "He's in the ministry, then?" Alimmus—" No ; in a restaurant. • Tut,: late Sir Robert Peel, speaking of Lord 1;;;,;un, remarked that "even his failings leaned .to virtue's' side ; " upou which a gentleman observed that his lordship's failings resembled the leaning. of PiAtt, Which, in spite of its long inclination, had never yet gone over. • • T.ns.:i.se is a school-house, on the window-sill of which is painted—it baying been a grocer's store; —"Powder and Shot." What the define have. powder and shot to do with, education?" "A great deal," replied a wag; "is it not the school- master's calling to teach the young idea how to shoot ? "

A " SHODDY " individual of New York, who has • recently been to Paris, writes that the " purtyest, portions of the city he has seen are the Bullyyards and the tooleries." He also says he was much Interested in the church they called the "Notry Dam. It is biggern half-dozen Old South's all in one." FEATHERLY had been cooling his heels for half an hour in parlour. Finally Miss Clara tripped its. • "You must excuse my delayed appearance, Mr. Featherly," she said, "but when your card was • brought to me I was engaged in sewing buttons on papa's coat." Before l'eatherly left he had fully committed himself. AT twelve the woman of the period wants to wear long dresses, with a train ; at sixteen she wants to be a great actress, at eighteen she wants a lover; at twenty-one she wants a husband; at twenty-five she wants him to stay at home in the evening ;.at twenty-eight she wants her own way; at thirty the Wants to be younger. "Iv is a curious custom the Japanese have, my dear," remarked a husband, "of taking off their shoes when entering the house." "The custom is curious," replied the lady, "from the fact that it is practised at all hours instead of at night only ;" and the husband said "Yes," with a rising inflec- tion, which was about all he could say. "DEAREST, believe me, I love you with my whole nervous organism. • You share with no other being the emotions which pervade my undivided grey matter, and, if I were conscious of a ganglion that throbbed not for thee, be sure I would not :sleep until I had procured its neurotomy.—Yours to the. last atom, --." " Wourpswounr," said Charles Lamb, "ens day told me that he considered Shakespeare greatly overrated. There is,' said he, an immensity of trick in all Shakespeare wrote, and people are taken by it. Now, ill had a mind, I could write exactly , like Shakespeare.' So you see," proceeded Charles Lamb, quietly, "it was only the mind that was wanting!" _ " You look so happy that I suppose you have •• 'been to the dentist and had that aching tooth pulled," said a man to a friend with a swollen jaw. It isn't that that mlkes me look happy. The tooth aches worse that ever, but I don't feel it." "How is that?" "Well, I feel so jolly because I have just been to the dentist, and he was out." Mar is a great thing. A few evenings ago a lady, who makes desperate endeavours to hold the fleeting charms of youth, asked a young gentleman to sing her a song, adding archly—" You haunt my dreams," or something equally complimentary. He struck into "The Last Rose of Summer," :bemuse, forsooth, it iiitted his voice. And now invitations from that house are known to him uo RIOTe• • MINISTER'S WIFE (looking over the paper)— "You are referred to in this morning' paper, my dear, as a distinguished clergyman.'" Minister —",ll.'m, I thought that my sermon yesterday would attract attention. Is it published in full or only a synopsis given ? " Wife—" Neither. You are spoken of as distinguished clergyman' in connection with that-patent medicine testimonial you sent to Dr. Quack." Mn. M•Lusir (slightly full)—" Now, my dear Maria, don't be severe on me. I've got a new conundrum for you. Heard it lasht night from one of the boys." Mrs. M`Lush (not at all mollified)—" Indeed." Mr. M`Lush—" Yesh. Lemma see—oh, yesh. • What lett the differensh between corned beef and cnrued men? You can't guessh that." Mrs. M'Lush (savagely)—" Yes, I Can. Because corned beef never makes a fool of tself."

CUARLES LAMB, who was somewhat troubled with an impediment in his speech—whose quips and quib'bles have been relished by many of us— while one day sitting at a public table had occasion to use a pepper-box. After shaking it with all due vehemence, and turning it in various ways, he found that the crushed pepper-corns were not inclined to come forth. " 1-t-h-this p-p-pe- pepper-box," he exclaimed, with a facetious grin "is something like myself." "Why io ?" asked a neighbour. " P-p-poor delivery," he replied. A COUNTRY PAPER says that one minister in that

place recently said th another: "I came near ' selling my boots to-day." The other marvelled, and made the brief but sage remark—" Ah Then seeing that further comment was expected, he asked, How was that ? " Then parson No. 1 sprung his trap: "Oh ! I had them half soled." Parson No. 2 is not expected to recover.

AN anecdote is told of a gentleman in Monmouth- shire which exhibits the pride of ancestry in a striking. point of view. His house ,was in such State of dilapidation that the proprietor was in danger of perishing under the ruins a the ancient rnancon, which he venerated even in decay. A sta auger whom he accidentally met at the toot of the Skyrrid, made various inquiries respecting the country, the prospects, and the Peighbouring houses, and among others, asked: "Whose is this antique mansion before Us?" " That, sir, is Werndee, a very ancient house; for out of it came the Earls of Pembroke of the first line, the Earls of Pembroke of the second line, the Lords He, berts of Cherbury, the Herberts of Coldhrook, Ramsey, CArdiff, and York, the Morgans of Acton, the Earls of liunsclon, the houses of Ircown and Lanarth ; and all the Powells. Out of this house also by the female line came the Duke of Beaufort." "And pray, sir, who lives there now 2" "I do, sir." "Then pardon me, and accept a piece of advice: Come out of it yourself, or you'll soon be buried in the t ulna of it." OF course a tall hat and tail coat count for some- thing, but a:growing boy never feels so really sure that he is getting to be a man as when he goes down town and the newsl oys rush up at him with the cry—"Ev'n. Citiz., sir I" OELFISHNESS is not an excess of self-love, and consists not in an over-desire of happiness, but in placing your happiness in something which inter- feres with, or leaves you regardless of, that of others.— Whately. EVERYWHERE I observe in the feminine mind something of beautiful caprice, a floral exuberance of that charming wilfulness which characterises our dear human sisters, I fear, throughout all worlcith—De Quincey.

Mr. Palgrave, tbe senior clerk a the tie, wig) presided ex-officio at the election of the Sligaiai: is alightly-bnilt, medium-sized man, closely-sh4ven, and about sixty years of age. He is,since thev4eath or Sir Erskine May, the greatest living authority on matters of Parliamentary practice. He is likewise an extremely erudite antiquarian and historian.

About two years ago his criticism of a picture at the Academy of the death of Charles I.—that the kneelihg position in which the King was depicted was incorrect, inashauch as Charles I. was beheaded lying on the ground—awakened a long and inter- esting controversy. His research also has -fixed the exact spot occupied by Charles L in Westminster Hall at his trial.,.

Miss Ellen Terry is staying at Win Chelsea, in the pretty cottage She bought from Mr. Cotayns Carr. Miss Terry is enjoying for a spell the comforts of home with her son, who is known in the playbills of the Lyceum by the name of" Gordon Craig,"and her daughter, who has so far, appeared only in amateur theatricals, in which she has taken part under the name of" Ailsa Craig." . , .

Not since Mr. Chamber-lai—n, a few weeks after the Pigott exposure, assured the, }louse of Commons that the Government were " forging their way," has a more painful metaphor been used than Mr. Goschen'sdebcription on Monday night of approach- ing fall of the Government as an" eviction." • Mr. Stuart, Renders house, near Guildford aZ which Mr. Gladstone has spent,rnore.than,one brief holiday, has the advantages of a beautiful situation and ,internal comfort, though it has no outward beaurYrof architectiire. With such acces- sions to individual families, says the journal, the; German Army will never be, in want' ef4e- crafts.

Sir Wilfrid Lawson on Tuesday afterncinn treated the Hciaselo one of the flashes of his caustic wit. On the sessional order forhidding.the interferice .of peers in elections being read from the,C'ham ir 'Wilfred inimediately rose in his place and asked the Speaker by what means could this order be en- forced, 4 The Speaker paused for a moment and seemed somewhat nonplussed by the" poser." He immediately, however, recovered himself and told the hon. baronet! that ,whep# any camp of the kind arose he could bring them under the notice of the House. Mr. Peel's deft answer was greeted with uproarious shouts of approval ( from tlko Tory benches. • Ai . !`t Tho most northern newspaper in the world is the " Nordkap," published at Hammerstein.-., The editor and hisussistants 'work in k smaltwobden house roofed with turf. News arrives to the " Nordkau " not by telegram but by the mail. boat, and the world's events reach the Hammersteiners very late, generally after eight days. The paper is published as we learn from the " Vossiche Zeitung,lonly once a week; SO that • the news is not unfrequently fortnight old. Much time is also lost in sending copies by beat to the different subscribeiiliving on the shores of the variousAords. Some subscribers fetch their newspapers themselves, and pay for them in kind, that is by herrings and other fish.

• The Spvernake estate, which will new pass into the hands of Lord I veagh, extends to about forty thousand acres. The rent is returned' as .£27,000 a year. There is not much of a hbuse, but the woods are almost unsurpassed in England, eiller for extent or beanty. This transacticii is thek biggest which has taken place in the land market for many years. Lord Illasham's complete purchases exceed it, but no single purchase of the, Manninghatn "silk king " comes near it. Swinton Castle cost him £140,000 and the Ailesbury estates in York- shire £310,000, which between them just make up the amount Lord Ireagb has paid for 'SaVernake At One time the late Colonel Tornline was anxious to sell the estates now owned.:by'his nephew for a million of money, but the price was prohibitive. , •

Lord Gerard has just acquired the Eastwell estate of the Earl of Winchilsea, .Eastwell Hall is a great ham of a place in Kent, commanding splendid views, and surrounded by about six thousand acres Wand. It cannot compare in attractiveness-with Beegebury, which is still unsold, aud which it is said Lord Iveagh would have bought if the appeal against the sale of Savernake had succeeded. Lod Gerard, who is a wealthy Lancashire colliery owner recently sold the well-known Aloulton Pad docks at NewmarLet Heath for .£.80,000. -He had not a big country house, a want expansively supplied by his new purchase. The Finch Hattons are understood to have more blood than money.

Has General Booth decided on establishing his first " over-the-sea colon." in liew Zeland ? It would seem so, seeing that a gentleman describing himself as "Staff-Captain Alderton, late superin- tendent of the farm colony on the Thames," has taken up his abode, with his wife and family, in Dunedin. In the course of an interview the staff- captain stated that General Booth had no intention of sending out any men who were not duly and properly prepared for the work that lay before them in New Zealand, The newcomer's arrival has attracted Parliamentary attention, and the New Zealand Premier has promised to subniitt for • th information of hon. mombers all the correspondence that has passed between the Government and General Booth.

, . el, THE EXTENSIVE THEFT OF JEWELLERY. On Saturday, at the Borough Magistrates' Court, I before Alderman Chandley (chairman), and Mr. R. Garnett, Wm. Rooney who had been previously hound over to appear again if called upon, on ac- count of hie having been found in suspicious pos- session of certain rings, was again placed in the•dock.: He was now charged with stealing from a railway van while in transit on the London and North-Western rail- way, from Warrington to Wigan, on the 16th -ult., a par- cel containing a quantity of jewellery, value £so.—Mr. Preston, barrister, of Chester, prosecuted on behalf of the London and North-Western Railway Company.— Thomas Sergeant, 'assistant to Messrs. Winstanley, jewellers, Wigan, said about 9.45 p.m. on the 16th ult., he despatched to Messrs. Constantine and-Floyd, Regent street, Birmingham, a box containing three sets of gold chains, studs and sleeve links combined, one set of links only, a solitaire, and a portion of another, two garnet rings, one wedding ring, one carbuncle ring, one lady's dress ring, and 'a brooch, all gold. He he=trd nothing more of the jewellery' till, 0, about ten days after, two railway detectives -showed him two rings produced, which he identified as his employers'.— William Taberner deposed to taking the parcel to Wigan station, and Francis Lawrenson to booking 'W by the 10.30 p.m. train to Newton, it being, he beliiied, the , only parcel he sent by that traia.—A porter testified to handing the parcel to the guard of the train, who also deposed to the receipt of it.—Joseph Byrne, assistant to Ann-Jackson, pawnbroker, 6; Winwick-road, said on the 18th ult. the prisoner brought the ring produced to pledge. He said it Was a present' to him, and he had had it about 12 months. The manager questioned him, and he then Said he had found the ring outside Chester. The police were then informed, and Detective-Sergeant Monaghan came, to whom the ring was handed, and the prisoner given into custody.—D.S. Monaghan said the prisoner told him on being arrested that he found the ring outside Chester. On scathing him at the station he found another ring, produced, in his coat pocket. Witness asked him hove he accounted for having it, and he replied "I only had the one." Then he added" I will tell you the truth. I was coming from Chester to War- rington on Saturday night last. I missed the station at Warrington, and got carried to a little place about seven miles from here : I believe they call it 'Newton. The , porter told me to get out of the train, as I had got past Warrington. „While I was waiting on thelelatform for the train to,Warrington I found a little box. I opened it and found two rings in it, wrapped in paper.' The priserletwas brought up at the court on tbel9th ult., and bound over ,to appear again if necessary, and on the 29th Ult. 'witness re-arrested him in consequence Of in- formation he received from Railway-Detective Osborne. The prisoner adhered to his lea statement" as to the rings, and said he knew nothing more about the matter. Harry Constantine, assistant to the consignees of the goods, deposed to the receipt of a communication an- nouncing the despatch of the parcel, but to its never coming to hand.—The prisoner. said he knew nothing about anything but the rings, and was committed for trial to the Liverpool Sessions.- a • _ •
A CRUEL INSULT.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUG vT OF SPARKS LOCOMOTIVE. I A FA.IIMER'S AGTION AGAINST A RAILWAY ' Court, COMPANY. `r- B. An action was lie-ard onllonday in the Liverpool 'IY County Court, before his Honour Judge Shand and a jury, in which Mr. Jotti Rimmer, farmer, of Huy- ton Hey, HuVon, sued the London and North:Wee-, tou Railway :Company for .229 2sj, the value Wu, waggon-And a load Of straw, the allegation being that these were destroyed by fire owing to negligence on the part of servants of the defendants. Mr. Florridge appeared for the plaintiff.--4t was stated that on the 23rd April last the waggons laden witti straWoneant for the Liverpool market, wai,crossing the bridge over the line at Broadgreen when there came from a locomotive beneath a number ot sparlm, which ignited the straw. The straw burnbd rapidly, so rapidly, indeed, that the waggoner could but barely save the horses, while of the waggon only a few bits of iron remained. Mr. Horridge speaking of the liability •of railway companies in such eases, said that a company was bound to construct itsl locomotives with all the appliances known to science for the purpose of preventing the emission of sparks. If this were done, a plait4iff had-to establish negligence on the part of driver or stoker. He contended that in this case the very quantity of sparks emitted, which would be spoken -of- by- indepettdeut-ituesses as .' myriads,: was in itself evidence of negligence. Mr. PiCkfoichirlto represented the defendant company, 'contended that tanless,-the .plaintiff 'could satisfy the 'jury that there Was negligence on the part of the corn- • pany:s servants, the' mere fact of sparkgbeing emitted and setting fire to the straw would not establish the liability of the company. The best constructed engines emitted sparks occasionally, and when this was not due ito Carelessness there was no liability at law.' His !Honour, irksurnming up, confirmed Mr.. Pickford's state- tnent of the law, that the construction of the engine not having been questioned, there was no liability upon the defendants unless the-plaintiff could show tnat there had been caaelessness in working the engine. The jury gave a verdict for the plaintiff for the ttmount claimed.. At the instance of the defendants' thd judge stayed execu- tion for a week, so that they might consider whether to appeal or not. , . .

In a Philadelphia court room, during the trial of an important spit invoiiihg certain ,fradellises, Benjiitnififfroister, afterwards Attornep;Geheral of the United States, was then the chief counsel of a Pennsylvania railroad company. Brewster was a frightfully ugly inan.-on'account.of a terrible dis- figurement of his face from burs but, intellect- ually; he was a giant, and, in deportment, a Chester- field. He Was: extremely sensitive' concering his facial misfortune, but never referred to it. The trial was a bitterly contested affair, and Brewster, at every point, got so much the best of the oppos- ing*Counsel that by the time the argume`rits dom- menced, his leading advecsary was in a white heat. In denouncing the railroad company, this lawyer, with voice tremulous with anger, exclaimed This grasping corporation is as dark, devious, and scarified in its, Method as is the lace of its chief attorney and henchman, Benjamin Brewster." This violent outburst of rage and cruel invective was followed by the breathless otilNess in the crowded court room that was painful: Hundreds of pitying ''es were rivethd on the poor, scarred face of 13rewSter, who sloWly arose and spokeisome- thing like'this'to the court: "Your Pono'Ut, in all my career as.alawyer.l have never dealt in person- alities; nor did I ever before feel dolled upon to ex- plain the,cause of -my physical misfortune vbirt I will do so now. When a boy, while playing around an open fire, one day, with 'a liitle sister, justlie- ginning to toddle, she fell into the roaring flames. I rushed to her resone, pulled her out before she was seriouSly hurt,i and fell into' the fire wadi. When they took rod oueof tliecoals'iny face *as as black as that man's, heart." The last sentence had an electrical effect; and the applatise that greeted it was superb; but, in an instant, turned to the most contemptuous hisses directed at the lawyer who had so cruelly insulted S. Louis (nobs Democrat."

div.head: RAFT ACCIDENT AT • ST. HELENS.
div.p: RAFT ACCIDENT AT • ST. HELENS.

TWO MEN DROWNED.—NARROW • ESCAPES. A serious accident, retulting in the drowning of 'two 'teen' and the narrow escapes of several others, occurred at Blackbrook, St. Helens. on Saturday afternoon. , The deceased men were employed as labourers by Messrs: Pilling and Co., the cOntrac- tors for the new Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancashire Railway, and the fatality occurred in the district known as the Double Locks, where a bridge, to carry the new railway over the Sankey Canal, some 14 or 15 yards wide, is in course of erection. For some weeks the men employed by the contractors have utilised a raft, made,of planks and measuring some eight or uire feetin•leng,th and about five feet wide, for crossing the canal and taking over their working material. Abotit noon on Saturday,'Mr. William Jones, of Worsley, near. Manchester, the cashier for Messrs. Pilling and Co., visited St. Helens, for the purpose of paying the laboarerd and other employe4 of the firm their wages. In accordance with the usual custom', he commenced at the 'St.-Helens end of the new railway works, and paid the men as he walked along the lines. He was accompanied by Mr. R. W. Friar, the local timekeeper, residing in Clipsley-lane, Hay- dock, and Police-constable Rothery, of Golborne, who is the supernumerary officer for the works, and is temporarily stationed at Ilaydock. These three men, who had in their possession a well. filled cashbox and bag, arrived in -due course at the raft crossing, and whilst they were being drawn aCross from the St. Helen to the Haydock side the deplorable accident occurred. A stout rope is attached to each dad of the raft; and the ropes are fastened to stakes driven into the embankments of the canal, in order that the raft can be dragged from either side, as may be desired. Mr. Jones, Mr. Friar, and the police officer got on the raft, and they were followed by a labouring navvy named George Jones, lodging at Blackbrook, and George Shepherd, another navvy, who lodged in Clipsley-lane, Haydook. Just as, the raft left the side another navvy nimed George Micklewright and a labourer, whose name is unknown, ran to the bank and jumped on to the raft. This caused the raft to tilt to one side, and someone shouted " Get to the, othe,r ;fieprly all the men immediately moved t&the bppoSite side, and the result waa that the, end quickly sank, and the seven men were thrown into, the middle of the canal which is eight or nine feetdeep. The scene which followed was very exciting. The men naturally struggled to save themselves, and whilst orte or two grasped the raft, others managed to reach the sides, where they were dragged out, thoroughly exhaust- ed; nyfellow-workmen who had witnessed the accident and rushed to the water's edge in order to render assist- ance. Most of the men wore heavyboota and elothing,and this fact rendered their position so extremely precarious that in the course of a few minutes two—Micklewright and Shepherd—lost their lives. Micklewright's bedywas dragged to the side 15 minutes after the unfortunate "'spin," but life was then extinct, and this proved to be the case with Shepherd, whose body was recovered five minutes latter. • • It lean interesting fact that the cashbox and bag, both of which contained large sums of money, were re- covered. Mr. Friar, the timekeeper, held the bag, and maintained his hold upon it when thrown into the water. Constable Rothery was carrying the cashbox in his ants when the raft upset, and it was thrown from his grasp, but luckify the box, said to be airtight and of patent construction,just floated on the surface and was easily saved. '

THE INQUEST. r ,On Monday nightjar. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Princess Royal Hotel, Park-road, St. Helens, on the bodies of George Micklewright, 70 years of age, of 170, Merton Bank-road,. and George Shepherd, 25 years of age, of Clipsley-lane, Haydock, labourers in the employ of the contractors for the new Liverpool, St. Helens, and South Lancaihire Railway, and who were drowned in the Sankey Canal, Blackbrook, by the upsetting of a raft on Saturday afternoon under cir- cumstances detailed above. Mr. Pickard attended on behalf of the contractors, Messrs. Pilling and Co.—After evidence of identification had been given, Police Con- stable Thomas Rothery, of the county police, employed as "supernumerary" for new works gave evidence. He said that ' every one was sober.—The Coroner: Is there any regulation for the working of this raft ?—Mr. Pickard: No, sir —The Coroner : I should think you'll now have some ?—Mr. Pickard : Yes, if it is thought necessary.—The Coroner: I daresay some one will think it necessary if you don't.—. Witness, said he had never known seven men to be on the raft at one time before. It was constructed by the contractors, and belonged to them.—Charles Morgan, labourer, said he was one of the last to get on the raft. Be had never seen seven men on the raft before, but he had frequently seen a much greater weight of material being taken a cross.—The jury retprned'a verdict that the men had died from an accidental cause, but recommended that the raft be made larger, and that proper regulations be posted for its use by the men. They also suggested that a handrail be placed along its centre.

div.head: UNHAPPY MOROCCO.
div.p: UNHAPPY MOROCCO.

Of written law there is none in Morocco. Prison- ers languish in chains, some innocent, some guilty but they are condemned without trial Or released; only through brihery (says a writer in the "Fort- nightly Review.") I find no security for life or property. The rich deny or bury their wealth, which is unearthed by threats and confiscated by torture. The poor lie down and starve. I see tribes of hardy mountaineers in constant 'revolt against the Sultan. I cannot see that the Sultan in any sense governs anything or anybody. He makes no reads, builds no harbours, fosters no trade, administers no justice; he only keeps his place by setting one tribe to plunder another, or by keeping, whole populations in a state of starvation, and hence unable to resist his exactions.

As he plays off the tribes within so be plays off the nations without. He keeps out their influence by fomenting, their rival, jeakmaies. In Tangier itself the diplomatic capital of Morocco, there is not a wheeled carriage. Why? Because there is not sufficient cohesion among the cOnsulates and legaJ, time to get a Carriage road made., This is called the status in quo, and is sometimes lauded as an admirable policy. Look beyond Tangier. I see between ranges of metalliferous mountaius, upon whose slopes herds of wild horses, enough to set Up the Continent with cavalry', or tame cattle for its commisariet could 'be raised, vast alluvial plains, well watered, utterly: untouched by industry, yet capable of bearing grain and fruit eirmgh to supply half Europe—wheat, oranges, !croons, Indian corn, sugar; grapes, olives, dates, bananas, and every kind of vegetable. 1 seq a great navigable river, the Lebo'', down which! all this produce might be, floated,-between Fez and the seacoast, for rapid export. Not a steam plough' or a harrow or a threshing machine will the ;titan permit; not a . square foot will ; not a steamer-or trading boat may ply upon rivers,which siMuld be at once the boundaries' of teeming and prosperous provinces and the arteries of cosmo- politan commerce.

In Whitworth Churchyard, conning the epitaphs at random, one specialising a model Facit house- wife catches the gaze. tier verse says This quiet life was truly hers, Her home the sum of all her cares • 'Twas there she laboured with her hands, And thus fulfilled St. Paul's:commands. , Perfection is discovered at times in this sublun- ary s'phere, for the cogitator is assured that Underneath this stone doth lie A* much virte as could die, Which when &live did vigour give To as much beauty as could live. We know not what a day may bring forth ; In the morning he rose in the fulness of health, , In the evening he fell in the paleness of death'.
Nay, full qf the vital spark, ,is instantaneously quenched - -the fate of a Shawforth operative:—
When I returned to work at noon No 4 thinkiag rieath would call me soon, A sudden stroke did take my breath, And laid me in the arms or death.

Once more:— • I was cut down like Cowers lain in the field By Him whose.arra can snake the world to yield. Upon the next stone is incised, under date Septem- ber 19th, 178.1, presumably by desire of James ,Stott, of Wardle • •" One hundred years, it now appear, Since corpse was first interred here •, When Viear's christian faith did hold, . And, minded Bibles more than gold. , My funeral rites to solemnise The priests refuse with specious lies ; Yet timely death shall soon declare How vile their worthless ashes are. It is surmised that relations between clergy and laity must have become acute to have called forth such a "stinger." PRIDE OF THE MILL,
THRILLING LOVE STORY. By LAURA JEAN LIBBEL
CHAPTER ITT.
"CAN YOU HEAR ME, DARLING ? " HER LOVER SHOUTED. "I WILL SAVE YOU, OR DIE 'lints- YOU I "

Oh, what was love made for if not the same Through joy and through torment, through glory and shame? Through the furnace unshrinking thy steps I'll pursue, And shield thee, and save thee, or perish there too.

BYRON. "Who are you 7" demanded the heiress, watching the lovely young face keenly. • • "I am lode Lawrence," answered the girl, her 'lips trembling. : "You cannot see him to-night, that 's certain," said Miss Elaine Granger, icily. " You should re- member a gentleman's residence is not the place to :call an business matters—that is, if it is a business 'matter you wish to consult him about. He has an ;office for that purpose; where you can find him usually during the day." The heiress turned haughtily away, and lonie i found the door closed summarily in her face. There had been an amazed listener to this dia- logue; no less a personage than Arthur Rochester - 'himself. He was coming down the broad stairway, his footfalls making no sound on the thick velvet carpet. Peters fell back in dismay when he saw his young master. "You were to take your orders from me when visitors called for me as to whether you were to admit them or send them away!" he said sternly. "Open that door." "Do you wish me to recall the person, sir 7" asked Peters, abashed. • "I will do so myself," said Arthur. "You forget, Arthur, that you are needed here to help receive our guests," cried the heiress, angrily. "What is this girl to you that you would follow ' her out in the storm 7 Is she some presumptuous I flame?" she added, with a keen touch of 'Spiteful- ness. The blood receded from Arthur's fuae aristocratic I face.

"Elaine—Miss Granger," he cried, "you forget yourself." "It is you who forget yomself," she retorted, with blazing eyes, "encouraging such creatures a§ that to come here to call for you, and disgrace the house."
Arthur Rochester gazed at the indignant, wrath- ful beauty in grieved amazement too deep for words; and in that one moment all brotherly liking he had for Elaine Granger died out of his heart.

"Stop I" he said, with stern reproof in his voice. "That young girl, although she works for a liveli- hood, is as noble a young girl as ever lived. God forbid that any one shall deem it a disgrace that she should enter this house."

"That's right," sneered the beauty, "champion the cause of the working girls." "I will just as long as I live," replied Arthur. "My respect for those honourable young ladies who earn their bread by honest work is profound; it is a proof, to every sensible man, that they amp and true."
iure4

Like a flash he was gene, leaving the heiress fairly quivering with rage and 'terrible jealousy. He quickly overtook the slim figure, and soon learned the cause cf. lonie's woe. ' "You shall return to the mill to-morrow," he saitV 44 I will be there in the morning myself. I will soon settle the matter. I missed you during your absence. I thought you had left the mill on your own account, Miss Lawrence."

He did not add how greatly he had missed her —that night and day he had been haunted by her sweet, pure face—and that he had found himself continually wondering if they should ever meet again. No bme can picture, indeed, how great was poor lonie's joy at the prospect of being reinstated in the mill. She thanked him in a voice choked with tears.
"It is not a seasonable hour for a young lady to be out alone, unattended," he said. "-You will permit me to place you in a coupe, and send you safe home."
lonic demurred; but firmly and gently be over- ruled her objection. He was too truly a gentleman of honour to take advantage of the situation and ride home with her.

He raised his hat with a grave, courteous bow as the coup rolled away, and turned his face home- ward. The heart in his bosom was beating strangely, and there was a tender light in his bonny blue eyes. That evening he moved about among the pleats with a happy smile on his lips. Pretty girls watched him with yearning eyes; coquettish belles did their best to flirt with the handsome young heir • but even while he talked with them, he was thinking of lonic, and how superior she was to these gilded butterflies of fashion. A month passed by. Ah mel how much can happen in a month. During that time, watching her from afar, Arthur Rochester learned to love lonie Lawrence with all the tree, manly" affection of his noble heart. Never was there such a bashful lover, though he loved so deeply; for never, by a word or look, had he betrayed the true state of his heart. He waited for an op- portunity to tell her of his love (forgetting that a bold wooer would have made his opportunity), and to ask her to share his heart and home.

rrank Lyons, his college chum, still lingered in the metropolis, and Arthur never once dreamed what the attraction was that kept him here. ' During that Month, Frank Lyons had managed to meet lonie often, always by accident, 'apparently, never by eppointmerit„ and to Sec her. home from the mill. Is it to ,he wondered, with no one to warn her, that her lonely, girlish heart drifted out to him? Once Mrs. Gtegory had met them to- getheA "Take care! Beware,. lonic sho had said that night. "The Man you Were walking with if as handsome as a prince, but I, do not quite like him. He !t; one of those fine, smooth-tongued aristocrats. I saw a big diamond sparkling in his bosom, and another on his band, white as a lady's, lie must be very wealthy. Take a word of advica from a I woman who has seen a good deal of life. 'Eagles 11 don't mate with sparrows,' or in other words, these wealthy young fellows don't often choose working-girls for wives, More 's the Pity. And there 's another old adage which it does no harm to remind young girls of, and that is, Never listen to words of love from a young man unless he speaks of marriage in the same breath." "But," argued lonic, with a beautiful little blush, "a young gentleman is not going to speak about love or marriage until be knowS a lady some little time, and finds oat whether he really likes her or not, I should fancy." .
"Be sure and not let your heart go out to him utitil you know his intentions, then," said Mrs. Gregory.

l3nt the heart in question had already gone out of lonie's keeping, with a love so great it frightened even herself; a . love that ends in a tragedy when the heart's idol is shattered and the love-dream broken.

At the end of that month a thrilling event happened. There had been important alterations of the left wall of the factory going on for a few days past, and for that reason the girls had been transferred to the fourth floor of the' building, among them lonie. It was noon, and for a brief hour the vast building seemed almost deserted, save for the few book-keepers in the main office, and two or three of the girls up on the upper floor, who had brought their lunch in preference to patronising the little restaurant round the corner. lonie sat apart from her companions, having finished her scanty repast, her curly head bent low over a book which she would not have cared to have the girls see. It was a bork on etiquette. Poor child She was eagerly studying the rules that regulated the deportment of the rich and grand young ladies whose society Frank Lyons must move.

Suddenly there was a low, hoarse rumbling like the sound of distant thunder. But Tonle was so deeply engrossed in her book she did not hear. 'lt's an earthquake 1" cried one. "No, no; the new wall is caving in!" cried another.

And, too terrified to even scream, they fairly flew down the nearest stairway to the street. There was another dull rumbling, followed by a terrific crash, that brought out all of the book-keepers, pale as death, to the pavement, but not an instant too soon. The stone wall fell in like the report of a hundred cannon, carrying the greater portion of the roof with it, and crashing down, down like a mighty cyclone, carrying all the il.sors and heavy machinery with it as it went. "Thank God the building is empty!" cried a

Now he read it slowly through, and as he read his face paled and he caught his breath hard. He leaned over and gave the bell-rope a vigorous pull, which brought Peters in breathless haste. "Is my son in the house ?" he asked, harshly- " If so, send him to me without delay." Miss Rochester, the mill-owner's maiden sister, heard that command, and knew, by the awful stern- ness of her brother's voice, that there was some- thing terribly amiss. • She went beraelf in search of Arthur, finding him in his own roma% . _ Your father wants you, my dear," she said- - "I am afraid something awful has happened, some- thing more than, the accident at the mill, for be looks so stern and so white, and tio very angrY• Be Is waiting for you in his library." "Waiting for me I" repeated Arthur. And a nervous sigh escaped him as he realised how unequal he was to a conflict with his stern father just then. His father was harsh and unyield- ing in his ideas... • It was his favourite expression that he had no patience with the frivolity of youth. Like many-a rich man, he clothed his son well. - for appearance's Sake, but he was extremely penuri- ous in money matters. He was always looking out for some trick or escapade of this handsome son of • his, for which he would have to pay. He did not give him credit for being as steady as be really was. • It was. little wonder that Arthur actually trem- bled as he knocked hesitatingly at his father's door. And he would have tremblea still more could he have seen the letter which his father, purple with rage, thrust away in his desk when he heard his Bout step. "Sit down," he said, brusquely. "I want to talk to you about Elaine Granger. This is no new sub- ject between us. Don't stand with your back to me looking out of the window. Do you hear or care for what I am saying 7" cried the millionaire raill- owner, thinking of the contents of the letter lying in his desk, and each moment his voice grew louder. and more excited. "Yes, father," answered Arthur, wearily, "I hear, I care, but I am so unsettled to-night. Let me off. won't you father, until another time—to-morrow, if you will." "No, I won't let you eff," declared Mr. Rochester, angrily. "I intend to know why you are so in- different to Elaine Granger, my ward. I will know,

Was the building empty? As if in answer, they heard a wild scream, and sonic one pointed upward. Simultaneously the vast thiong assembled below raised their eyes, and be- held the figure of a young girl clinging to the shak- ing timbers on the topmost floor. Terror and despair were written upon every feature of the beautiful, childish face turned to- wards them.

They saw her lips move and they knew it was a wild, agonising prayer for help, although the noise of the falling rocks drowned her piteous voice. She was so young, so fair, to die! Could nothing be done to save her? was the cry on every lip. Yet there was not one who dared brave death in that falling structure, and the vast crowd stood by as if petrified, unable to act or move. Besides, they saw, to their, horror, one of the great wheels of the machinery, just above her head, 're- volving with lightning -like rapidity, and which must soon give way. No poWer, save the hand of God, could keep it from falling upon her .and crushing her before their very eyes. Even the spiral iron stairway—the only means of reaching the poor girl—swayed to and fro on its fastenings, awaiting but another avalanche of stones to send it whirling dawn with the rest of the wreck. No man dared trust. his weight upon it; and then the wheel—to be in its path one moment more would mean certain death.

The crowd below saw this, and realised it. Strong men turned away with hoarse, shuddering cries. Women fainted outright, their bitter cries mingling with the hoarse rumble that shook again through the doomed wall.

Looking down at the surging mass of horrified faces,. bole saw but one—the face of Frank Lyons, her lover—and to him, in that vital moment of life or death she looked for help. But he shrank back. "No! no 1" he „panted hoarsely to himself. "I could never risk' my life to save hers. It is not to be thought of." " Back ! Give me room 1" cried a clarion voice in the crowd.

A young man who had just appeared on the scene took in the situation at a gl.inzo. "Back 1" he commanded, in a voice like a bugle blast; and the crowd parted. In a flash he had sprung up the swaying spiral stairway to the gjrl's rescue. "Oh, God 1" was the cry of an hundred voices in the crowd. "It is Mr. Arthur Rochester 1"

r say. " Elaine leaves for boarding-school nest week, and of course you have taken advantage of the 013- - portunity her visit to your aunt afforded you by proposing to her, haven't you? " " For Heaven's sake, father, let me attend to raY own love affairs," replied• Arthur, turtling delidit
"Come back I come back r they cried in terror. "It means death. Better one should die than two."

But he heeded- them not. Up, up the swaying stairs he spraug, his face blanched when he saw the horrible wheel; but he pushed onward. ' " lonie I" he called. "My poor girl, can you hear me and understand? I have come to Save you, or die with you." , , • , , . ,

"What are you fooling around for 7 " Arthur Rochester turned slowly and faced las father. "I will answer you truly, honestly, and honour- ably, father," he said. div.p: should also be made into the condition of evicted tenants, and he did not see why an effort should not be made to shorten the punishment of certain convicts. The debate was, after further discussion, adjourned on the motion of Mr. Leveson Gower. HOUSE OF COMIIONS.--Tnirsimx.
The House presented an. unusual spectacle when the Speaker took the chair at three o'clock.
A CROWDED 110t'SE.

Even before prayers were read not only was every seat on the floor filled, but the galleries also, especially on the Ministerial side, were crowded with members. After prayers the scene became even more striking, as the strangers' and ladies' galleries become filled to over- flowing, and, a much rarer occurrence, the'peers' en- closure was not eufficient for the members of the Upper House who wished to secure seats there. Prominent among these were Earl Spencer, -Lord -Runts/ord, Lord Camperdown, Lord Ashbourne, Lord Sandhurst, Lord Nelson, Lcrd Montague, and the Bishop of Ripon. Mr. Gladstone entered the House from behind the Speaker's chair immediately after Archdeacon Farrar had concluded the reading of prayers, and was greeted with prolonged cheers from the Liberals and Nationalists. Some little time was devoted to swearing in of members, among those who took the oath being Sir John Lubbock, Mr. W. Redmond, Lord Elcho, Mr. Bartley, and Mr. Aird.

div.head: NO CONFIDENCE DEBATE.
div.p: THE NO CONFIDENCE DEBATE.

Mr. GLansrofts continued the debate on the " No confidence" resolution. He complained that tbe Govern- ment had laid no policy ,before the House, characterised the charge that the Liberal majority was made up from one section of the kingdom as a weak one, and main- tained that the majority was gained on Borne Rule. Turning to Ireland, the right hon, gentleman said the Coercion Act ought not to be retained on the Statute Book one moment longer than was required by the con- ditions of the country; and as regarded the amnesty question, it was impossible, he said, for those who were not responsible Ministers to give any pledge or under- taking to deal with criminal cases either in respect of revision of sentences or of the prerogative of mercy, be- cause that could only be performed by those who had full knowledge of the facts. With respect to the evicted tenants, should arrangements not be come to duriag the autumn between them and the landlords, legislation might become requisite. The Home Rule Bill would provide for a full and effective maintenance of the supremacy of the Imperial Parliament, would enable Ireland to manage her local affairs, and should the House of Lords reject it, it would be impossible for any Government to regard such rejection as terminating its duties. He then proceeded to refer to the needs of Great Britain, which, he said, would be adequately dealt with. Mr. Batsona, after stating that he had refuted until he was sick of doingso the astonishing fables regarding Ireland which Mr. Gladstone had continually put for- ward, proceeded to deal with the accusation which had been levelled against the Government of not following precedent in calling the House together for the present debate, and asked,* if the Government had lost the con- fidence of the House, who had obtained it? The Liberal party had been conquered by gentlemen below the gangway, and if Mr. Gladstone and his friends carried out all their promises with regard to Home Rule, they would make themselves a laughing stock for the world. Mr. T. P. O'Connor accused Mr. Balfour of using language inciting to a revival of crime in Ireland, while Mr. T. W. Russell said that whatever form Home Rule took under a Liberal Government Ulster would resist it even to the death.
—..- Sir 11. MEYSEY THOMPSON followed, after which Mr. Naoroji made his maiden speech. A number of other members took part in the debate. . . .

At a quarter to twelve o'clock Mr. CHAMBERLAIN moved the adjournment of the debate until Thurs- day. Mr. T. HEALY protested ogainst the time of the House being wasted by the adjournment over Thursday. It was a piece of jobber'? by the outgoing Government. The hon. member was proceediwa' to say that some forty revising Tory barristers had been appointed since Saturday, including the rospective son-in-law of the Irish secretary—(lrish cheers)—when Mr. JACKSON rose to say there was not the slightest foundation for the shameful allegation made by the hon. member. (Government cheers.) Mr. HEALY said he had it on the authority of the Orango organ. (Irish cheers.) Mr. JAcxsox said it was in the "Freeman's Journal." Mr. HEALY said that if what he had said was unfound- ed, he had great pleasure in attenuating it to any ex tent but the substance of the argument remained. The Government were wasting time for the purpose of per- petuating jobbery. (Irish cheers.) Earl COMPTON said they were quite prepared to vote at once. The country would view the dragging out of the question with discontent and dissatisfac- tion. The motion was carried without A division, and The debate was accordingly adjourned until Thurs- day. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUURSDAT.
THE DEBATE IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS. DECISIVE DEFEAT OF THE GOVERNMENT.

In the House of Commons on Thursday there was such &large attendance of members that for the first time for many years chairs had to be placed on the floor of the ,House below the gangway. The Peers' and Strangers Galleries were also filled. Notices_for next session were given by Mr. A. C. Morton and Dr. D. H. Macfarlane; and a number of questions were put in reference to affairs in Afghanistan and the Straits' Settlement, the loan to British Columbia, the British Mission to Morocco, inoculation for pleuro-pneumonia, free coinage in India, &c. The debate on the no confidence amendment to the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne was resumed at twenty minutes past four by Mr. Chamber- lain, who first pointed out that the Liberal Unionists had come back a party 43 strong, soon to be increased to 49—a thing which had never before happened to a third party. They remained a political force whose in- fluence in the country was not to be measured by their influence in that House. The member for Midlothian, he continued, had spoken of the debate as the most singular in the records of the House, I and he agreed with him in that, and also in his state- ment that the issue between the Unionist and the Home Rule party had been decided by the country. But he could not admit that it gas, under the circumstances, irrelevant to do anything more than expel the present I Government from office, without any regard to the orovernment of the future, which, with something more than his usual felicity of expression, the right hon. gentleman had described as a nebular' hopothesis. For the next five or six months the nebular hypothesis was going to carry on the whole administration of the coun- try, and to decide its policy, and the opinion of the House of Commons could not be taken upon it. Refer- ring to what he called the conspiracy of silence on the Liberal benches, he asked whether the Welsh members, whose great cry was the disestablishment of the Church, had got any assurance upon that question. Their prospects were not promising, in view of Mr. Redmond's mandate that no question was to be brought forward which would be likely to distract attention from Home Rule. He proceeded to quote from speeches de- livered by Sir W. Harcourt and Mr. Gladstone, in which both right, hon. gentlemen had declared in favour of the supremacy of the British Parliament. But the Irish Nationalist party had always demanded in the strongest possible terms that the Irish Parliament should be abso- lutely supreme in regard to the affairs committed to it, and that no veto upon its acts should be exercised on the advice of the English Goverment. The result would be that there would be in office for the next six months a Government which, if it kept faith with England, would ensure the hostility of the Irish Nationalist party, and the incoming Government, instead of being in a majority I of 40, would be in a minority of 150. The debate having been continued by, among others, Mr. Macartney, Sir John Lubbock, the Solicitor-General. Mr. S. Wood., and Sir Henry James, the House divided, 1 with the following result For the amendment Against
Majority against Government 40 Cn the motion ot Mr. Balfour, the House then at 12.25 adjourned till Thursday next.

div.head: COLONIAL NUR FOR M.P.'S.
div.p: A COLONIAL NUR FOR M.P.'S.
EXTRAORDINARY' PROPOSAL.

The "Daily Chroniele " says :—We learn that a well- known member proposes on some convenient occasion— probably when the next Naval Estimates come on—to move that the Admiralty be instructed to place one or more of her Majesty's troopships at the disposal of the House for the purpose of conveying such members as care to avail themselves of the opportunity on an Im- perial trip to the chief British colonies. The fact that the originator of this novel idea is a Scotchman seems to preclude the supposition that it is a joke. If it is to be taken seriously, we have seen much worse legislation at Westminster. It is indisputable that the large majority of members who are called upon to legislate for the em- pies have hut the vaguest idea witat this "empire" really is, and that the sight of it would be a revelation to them. In fact,one or two officials outside Parliament would be much the better for seeing a little of the coun- tries they rule so confidently. The expense of such an ' Imperial education tour would not be very great, and of course the members would be received with the greatest enthusiasm everywhere. The Canadian Pacifla would take them gratis across Canada,and in most places they would be entertained at public cost. Supposing 300 went,itwould be an advantage incalculable in money to diffuse the in- formation that they would bring back throughout the country. Then there wpuld be only one foreign policy and the office of the Foreign Secretary could be made non-party. That, perhaps, is the dream of the sugges- tor. At any rate, he believes that every member would come back, like himself, a Radical Jingo. It is not im- possible that something may come out of the sugges- tion.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 13, 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 13, 1892.
T E RRIBLE FALL AT ST. HELEN.
A W ARRINOTON " STE EPLEJACK " K I LLE D

A " steeplejack " named 'Ralph Woods, of War- , Alas:ton, met with a terrible death at St. Helens on Monday night. Woods and a fellow-workman named John Mains, of Warrington, were in the employ of Messrs. S. P. Bidder & Co., chimney builders and re- pairers, Cheetham-hill, Manchester, who a week or two ago contracted to carry out some necessary re- pairs to a chimney at the copper works of Messrs. Newton, Keates; St Co., near Sutton Oak Station, St. Helens. This chimney was erected to the height of lE33ft. in 1882,and in stormy weather during the last few months bricks and stones have occasionally fallen from the top. The repairs were commenced last Monday week, and all went well until Monday afternoon, when Woods and Mains appeared to resume operations. This was the first time either of the men had been employed on the job, and, contrary to expectation, they did not arrive until half-past four. From statements made by the man Mains on Monday night, it appears that early in the morningpe and Woods left Warriugton,where they both resided, intending to walk direct to St. Helens They called at Earlestown,where,owing to the inclement weather, they stayed for several hours. The journey was resumed in the afternoon, and they ultimately ar- rived at their destination. The men immediately decided to ascend the chimney, and did so in the usual way,viz., by the ladders attached to the outside of the chimney, and left so affixed by the workers on the job last week. They remained at the top about a couple of hours, and a quantity of broken bricks and stones was thrown down. At half-past six the men descended and visited the , Queen's Arms Hotel, kept by Mr. William Barrow, and asked to be supplied with some drink. For obvious realms, however, Mrs Barrow declined to serve them, and the we men departed. About half an hour later- both returned to the works and again— mounted to the top of the chimney. Their operations soon attracted a crowd of some hun- dreds of persons to the vicinity of the works, and it was a general remark that the men went about their work with considerable vigour, if not with a degree of daring. About half-past seven one of the men was seen to push over some stones and bricks, and directly afterwards was seen to stagger. A moment later the onlookers were horrified to see him fall headlong to the ground, and after turning round in its descent, the body alighted with a thud on the ground. Several persons at once ran to the spot, and found that the unfortunate man's body was terribly mangled. His skull had dropped on the edge of a brick, crushing it into the earth ; and an ex- amination by Dr. Bates, who was summoned, revealed the fact that every bone in the lifeless body was smashed to pieces. Information was at once convey( d to the police authorities, and Police-sergeant Brooks and Con. stables Filingham and Bradbury removed the body to the Manor Arms Hotel to await the inquest. The de- ceased man, Ralph Woods, was 30 years of age, and is supposed to have lodged at the house of his father-in- law, in Oliver-street, Warrington. He leaves a widow and some children, but it is stated that his own home was broken up a weak or two ago. He only returned to work on Monday after a month's stoppage. Mains, his fellow workman, stated that he and the deceassd were working back to back at different sides at the top of the chimney. Deceased was using a small crowbar, and Mains supposed that in pushing over the bricks and stones Woods overbalanee& himself, or his clothing caught a portion of the debris, causing him to fall to the bott.m. He did not see the occurrence, but heard Woods call out, "Oh, dear." He immediately turned , round, and Wood then disappeared. A crowd of some thousands of persons gathered in the neighbourhood of the copper works, and the shocking occurrence was, of course, the sole topic of conversation.

THE INQUEST. Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, held an inquest at the Mona Arms, Sutton, St. Helens, on Wednesday, on the body of Ralph Woods, a steeplejack, aged twenty- seven years, who lived at 13, Turner-st., Warrington,but who was killed by falling from a chimney, 181 feet high at Messrs. Newton and Beata's copper works. Mr. Smith, manager, represented the copper company, and Mr. S. P. Bidder, chimney contractor, of Manchester, who was doing the work of repairing the chimney, was also present. John Mains, of Warrington, who was working with., deceased at the time the accident oecurred, said they left Warrington by ; train at half-past nine on Monday morning. They stayed at Earlestown until two o'clock, when they had two pints of beer. They walked on to ISt. Helens, where they had another pint of beer. They started work at four o'clock. The chimney was eleven feet in diameter, and had nine inch brick work. They worked about an hour and a half, and came down. They had no money with them, and intended to ask the foreman to lend them some money to get something to eat until next day. The foreman had left, but a labourer said to them that he would show them where the foreman got drink, and they would perhaps get some. They went to the Queen's Arms, but Mrs. Bar- row refused to serve them. Witness thought the reason ' was because they had got no money. They afterwards went to another public•house and got a pint of beer each. The labourer bad then lent them sixpence. He I did not recollect Mrs. Barrow saying to Police-sergeant Brooks that the reason she would not serve them was because they had had enough. They went up the ' chimney again and worked for about half-an-hour. Wit- ness told Woods not to take too much off at once, but dolt gradually, and he replied, " Get on with yours, and I'll have mine off before you." Witness turned round to his work, when deceased shouted" Oh, my," and was gone. He did not think that he had had too much beer, and did not show signs of intoxication. The Coroner : Were both of you playing fool on the top of the chimney. Witness: No sir. We were doing nothing unusual so as to attract the people round. We were doing our work well, and did not show any bravery at all. A Juryman: How many stones did you threw off before you got a plank up as a scoffold. I was watching you. Mr. Bidder: It is not necessary to put planks up at all. They had to throw one part off before planks could be put up. The Coroner (to witness) : Then you had four pints of beer, according to your own showing. Witness: Yes, during the day. The Coroner: And three and a half pints too much. Now, what do you'say was the reason of this man's fall ? Had he too much drink ? was he experienced enough, or was it because you had not proper appliances? WitnesS: I' suppose it was a pure accident. Be over- did himself with lifting toe much off at once, and went with it. Mr. Bidder said the men were provided with rules They had to sit on the top of the chimney, and take off one course at a time. There was no reason why the deceased ought not to have been perfectly safe. He was a naturally careless, reckless man, and would walk round the tops of chimneys. There was plenty of room for them to walk on the top. The projection was one foot two inches, and with nine inches of brickwork there would be two feet. The man was doing the work in the usual way recognised by the trade. It would be more risk to put up a scaffold, as a large stone falling on the scaffold would bring it and the men down together.

A in-yin-in : I think there is some neglect. _ TI eat ‘;).! •;.:er ; I don't think you ought to express a dir op i ...,o like that. It is very unfair. I don't thin, Ina lan't lay with the maoner in which the work was idone. The men had 11;1,1 too much beer. They don't fence round chimneys, and they don't fence round public-houses. Mr. Bidder: I Delieve the man has lost his life in going at it in a reckless way, trying to get too much off at once and please me. I don't think he had too much beer. Four pints to these is very little indeed. The Coroner: Is there anything that you could have put up to prptect these men ? Mr. Bidder : No sir. As I have said, he was a man of reckless habits, and he has lost his life through foolhardi- ness. The jury, after deliberating about a quarter of an how; returned& verdict of "Accidental death," without adding any Aden
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. It. Heaton presided, and there were also present, the Rev; G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Balharry, Davies, Rib- bee, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, Muir, Fairclough, Hum- phreys, Ratcliffe, Mather, W. Houghton, Smith, Dignum. Shaw, Filling; J. C. Button (clerk) and other officers.

div.head: GIFTS.-YISIT OF THE MAYOR AND HAYORISS.
div.p: GIFTS.-YISIT OF THE MAYOR AND HAYORISS.

The Workhouse Master reported that the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs. Greensll) had called at the Workhouse and brought flowers and fruits for the inmates. The Mayoress went through the house and expressed herself pleased with all she saw. Mrs. Fran- comb had al sp very kindly sent miscellaneous reading for the inmates, and a quantity of flowers had been received from St. Paul's mission. The Superintendent of Padgate Schools reported gifts of " Graphics " from Mr. Balshaw of the White Bull Inn,and from Mr. Evans, of the Coopers Arms, Bewsey-at. •

div.head: BEGISTRATIO!q OF 11•YDOCK.
div.p: BEGISTRATIO!q OF 11•YDOCK.

_ The CLERK read the following letter, which had been received from the office of the Registrar-General :—" In further reference to your letter of the 13th inst., lam directed by the Registrar-General to inform you that the proposal of the Guardians has had his careful considera- tion, and he finds himself unable to comply with their request and sanction the change they desire in the New- ton registration sub-district. It must be borne in mind that the addition of a registration sub-district involves increased cost, both as regards that portion of the ex- pense of registration that is defrayed by the Exchequer anti the residue that is chargeable on the local rates. The district of Warrington is at present sub-divided into six sub-districts, and it would appear desirable rather to decrease that number by amalgama- tion, as opportunity occurs, than to form additional sub- districts. The population of the existing sub-district is only 19,398 which is well within the scope of one regis- trar with properly arranged stations and attendances. The population of flaydock urban sanitury district which it is proposed should be formed into a separate sub-district is only 8,536 and has, perhaps, two deaths a week, so that if the registrar attends there twice a week—as he will be directed to do—there can be no necessity for any inhabitant to travel outside the town- ship for registration purposes, seeing that in cases of necessity deaths can be provisionally registered by communicating with the registrar by letter. lam to add that it appears that the present sub-district and the relief district are co-terminous, and from a registration and statistical point of view it is very desirable they should so remain."—Mr. Ratcliffe thought it was rather hard on a rising township like Flaydock that the request it had made for a separate registrar should be retused.—The Clerk remarked that the registrar-general would, of course, in dealing with that case take a broad view of the whole country. If the Haydock people were not satisfied they might get their member of Parliament to use his influence with the Government. —Mr.Balharry said that Mr. Legh, M.P., had already moved in the matter,and they had had two letters.
-A.VP^INTMENT OF A NORM. On the z ecommend4ion of the House Committee,Miss Alice Cavanagh, of Mrnchester, was appointed a nurse at the Workhouse at a salary of £25 a year. This was all the business.

div.head: SWIMMING IN MANACLES.
div.p: SWIMMING IN MANACLES.

Professor Jules Gautier accomplished a remarkable feat on Wednesday in swimming from Folkestone to Dover, about eight miles, with his hands and feet manacled, although the sea was somewhat rough and unfavourable. Gautier started from Victoria Pier, Folkestone, at 12.10 p.m. in the presence of a large con- course of people. He successfully accomplished the distance, reaching Dover at 4.10 p.m. The tide turned before the swim was accomplished, and Gautier had some difficulty in making any progress during the last half-hour.

div.head: MELTING SNOW OBSERVED IN MARS.
div.p: MELTING SNOW OBSERVED IN MARS.

A despatch has been received in New York from Pro- fessor Pickering, of the Harvard Observatory at Are- quipa, Peru. He says, with reference to his observation of Mars in opposition:—" There eems to be two large areas near the equator of Mars which are of a permanent blue colour. The total size of these two areas is 500,000 square miles. On June 23 small dark spot appeared on the southern snow cap, and later this spot length- ened rapidly. Early in July it was 1,000 miles in length, and divided the snow cap in halves. The snow has melted from an area of 1,600,000 square miles in the last thirty days. Small dark areas surrounded by snow appeared on July 10. On July 12 I saw a dark forked line in the form of the letter " Y" in the direction of the seas. On the 16th a dark area appeared on the northern side of the stem of the" Y" which connected the northern seas. On the 24th a dark area like a lake appeared near the snow line. On the 25th the southern branch of the "Y" became very narrow. Many other minor changes appeared, and on Monday night of this week I observed a bright green area near the pole.

Festivities are being arranged throughout Hungary to celebrate the 00th birthday of Louis Kossuth. The Postmaster-General announces the extension of the express delivery service in London to eighty-one other post-offices. The Blackburn borough engineer reports that an out- lay of £170,000 is necessary to provide for the future demands on the water supply of the town. _

Glandemit seems,is spreading very rapidly in London, and last week's returns of the Registrar-General contain the announcement of one death from this malady. THE LATE REV. S. KENWORTHY.

The funeral took place on Saturday of the Rev. S. Kenworthy, the late pastor of Hill Cliff Baptist Chapel. The remains were interred in the burial ground at Hill ChM The cortege left the deceased's late residence shortly after 2.30 in the following order :—Hearse and bearers—Messrs. J. Bradford W. Hough, Walker, A. Walker, W. Arnold, and J. Grounds; Mr. Arthur Kenworthy, and Masters James and 'Lawrence Kenworthy (sons of the deceased), Mr. James Kenworthy (brother), Mr. Thomas Hough (cousin) ; Mr. W. Bradford, Reddish Hall, (uncle) ; Dr. Willett; Rev. Mr. Maiden (Inskip near Preston), Rev. John Yonge, Rev. J. W. Varley (Latchford); Rev. C. J. Rolfe (curate-in-charge, St. Thomas' Stockton Heath), Rev. J. Davies (Cockhedge Mission), Mr. Robert Davies, and a number of other friends. On reaching Hill Cliff the coffin was taken into the church, and the organist (Mr. Harrison) played the recit., "I know that my Redeemer liveth." After the singing of "Rock of ages cleft for me," the Rev. John Yonge read the first portion of the service for the burial of the dead. Mr. Yonge afterwards addressed the large congregation present, and in the course of his remarks he said they were assembled, with feelings of , deep and sincere sympathy, to consign to their last earthly resting place the remains of a Christian man and a Christian minister. They met there not only with the members of his bereaved and sorrowing family, but In the Midst also of the Christian com- munity, among which he spent the only too brief years of his pastoral work. They were about to bear his body to its tomb among his own kindred, and in his own place of birth and latest service. To him, personally, it was a source of much regret that he whom all present knew so well, and whom they were so truly sorrowing about that day, was to himself com- paratively a stranger, save by very slight acquaintance, and by his knowledge of his deserved reputation as an earnest and consistent minister of the gospel. When, however, he was requested to discharge the service on that occasion which their well-known friend, Dr. Parker, was unable to undertake, he felt alike the compulsion of duty and the willinghood of deep sympathy with the bereaved family, and a neighbourly esteem for the sorrowing church and people. The death of their brother inevitably filled with sorrow and sadness the hearts of all who knew him ; and very especially their hearts who knew hire by the tender names of husband, father, brother, and personal friend. The members of that flock were also grievously distressed at the swift and unlooked for ending of what they hoped might have been a protracted and useful pastorate. Little, he sup- posed, did any of them imagine when on the previous Sunday they were enjoying his services that that was, in the will of God, his farewell Sabbath in their midst. As little, probably, did he imagine it himself, thinking, as he (Mr. Yonge) was told he did during the days be- fore that• Sunday, that he was in stronger health than he had been for a long time. It had, however, been noted since his death than never did he appear more intensely in earnest in his preaching than on that last Sunday. It was said, and it would be la the recollection, doubtlessof , all who heard him, that he then represented himself as speaking as a dying man to dying men,and as being inten- sely desirous that the blood of the souls of his hearers should not rest upon him. He pleaded with his hearers as earnestly as though he had felt he would never plead with them again. Still,it might not have been from any clear consciousness, but only from what was to him at the time unaccountable impulse, that his words assumed that solemn tone. How little any ef them knew how near might be the wondrous moment when they might be called upon to cross the confines of the unseen ! That was the funeral of a Christian man ; and one who, as he learned from his brother, began in earl life to think and feel and speak about the truths of Christ ? Before the age of 20 their friend commenced preac;iing, and speak- ing also in the cause of temperance, being, in his young manhood, secretary of the Temperance Society at Pro- vidence Chapel, Stockton Heath. His lot was cast at Manchester from 20 to 25, and there, with several others attending Dr. McLaren's church, he formed a society for self-improvement, and Christian usefulness. Some of the members afterwards became ministers, among others being Mr. Maden, now Baptist minister at Inskip, near Preston. On leaving Manchester and going to Tunstall, in Staffordshire, Mr. Kenworthy became a local preacher, scarcely ever missing a Sunday in active preaching duty among the Methodists for some twelve years. He afterwards served as a preacher for four years among the Baptists at Burslem and neighbour- hood. During this period he was engaged in active business pursuits, living a quiet and friendly life, doing all the good he could, and making, as he was told, hosts of friends wherever he went. Of his four years as pastor of that church he had no need to speak. Most of those present had been, more or less witnesses of his " work of faith, and labour of love." less, of them, as he could only believe, would have lifelong occasion to bear in loving memory as one who did his best to minister to their spiritual needs, comforting them in their sorrows, seeking to lead them nearer to Jesus Christ. &me of them might even owe to hire, under God their very conversion. Their deepest sympathy was due to his widow in her sorrow, left with so large a charge, and to his fatherless children. In faith and prayer they commended them to the Divine Husband of the widow, the Divine Father of the fatherless. As the years. advanced the circle of their relationships and friendships perpeteally contracted. The family of their departed brother were feeling this afresh that day. Not long since the aged head of the family was carried to his tomb, and nos,- the youngest of his sons was following him. Viewed from the earthly standpoint, these events were inevitably distressful. Death created large vacancies in hearts and homes ; va- cancies that no earthly resource could supply. How well it was that wherein earth failed heaven succeeded. What they lost in their fellows they might ever find in God. _

The processiox afterwards moved on to the burial I ground, and as the mourners left the church Mr. Harri- son played the Dead March in "Saul." At the graveside the Rev. John Yonge read the concluding part of the service, and the hymn, "Shall we meet beyond the river ?" was sung, after the coffin had been lowered into the grave. A number of beautiful wreaths were contri- buted by the following :—Mr. and Mrs. Whitley, Mrs. Dodd, Mrs. Carter, Mr. and Mrs. Worrell, Mr. and Mrs. T. Hough and family (Acton), Mr. and Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Blackhurst (Tunstall), Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Hough (Acton), Mr. and Mrs. Cumberlidge (Tunstall), the mem- bers of the deceased's family, Mr. and Mrs. Booth and family, Miss M. J. Lawless, and Mr. and Mrs. J. Moss.

The living of Dunton, Essex, of the annual value £425, has become vacant through the resignation of the Rev. W. 11. Tucker, who has held it since 1845. The rev, gentleman, though in his ninety-third year, is in the enjoyment of fairly good health.

Owing to advice given by Mr. H. M. Stanley and the Committee of the Church Missionary Society the pro- posed scheme for a Soudanese Christian Mission has been abandoned for the present. Mr. F. J. Williamson, sculptor, of Esher, has had the honour of submitting to the Queen, at Osborne, a marble bust of Princess Victoria Eugenie of Batteaberg which he has executed for her Majesty.
