div.head: HO'ARD AND TILE STANDARD OF WAGES.
div.p: THE HO'ARD AND TILE STANDARD OF WAGES.

The Clerk read the following letter from the Secretary of the Widnes District Tractes Council :—" 112, Mersey- street, August Bth, 1892. To the Chairman of the Widnes Local Board. Dear sir,—Some little time ago your Board passed a resolution to the effect that in the future all work done by the Board should be paid for at the prices recognised in the district. and I have been instructed by the above Council to call you; attention to an infringement of that resolution, as we have been given 0 understand that a labourer is now employed by the Board as a bricksetter at 50. per hour, building man- holes. We need scarcely remind you that although the work being done is out of sight, it is only reasonable to suppose that it cannot be expected that the work will be done in a workmanlike manner, being done by an incompetent man and must necessarily be dearer in the end. Hoping your Board will look into the matter, I remain yours truly, A. G. LOWREY.

div.head: GAS- AND W &TER COMMITTER.
div.p: GAS- AND W &TER COMMITTER.

This Comraittee's report contained the following : Gas Testing.—Report of tests on the 19th and 25th ult., read: Illuminating powers, 15.19 and 16.20 candles. B)ard'a Seal.—Recommendel that the seal of the Board be affixed to contract with Messrs. W. and J. Richard- son, for the supply of gas coal. Engineer's report dated this day read as follows :—"Netherley Extension— Building Contract—Satisfactory progress has been made with this work during the past month, the raof having been boarded over and the slating is now being pro- ceeded with. It will, however, take from three to four weeks longer to finish the whole of the work in connec- tion with the building, but this can be executed with- out any interfeence with the workmen engaged erecting Dhe engine and pumps. Contract for Engine and Pumps —Messrs. Ilathorn, Davey and Co. have four fitters and eight labourers engaged on this work. The travelling , crane in the engine room and the winch in well room have been fixed. The engine and force pump bed, also the frame and slide bars belonging to the quadrant motion of the bore hole pumps have been laid down. The high and low pressure cylinders are in position and partly fitted with gear. The whole of the materials in connection with the engine and force pump are de- livered, but some little delay is anticipated in the de- livery of the 18" wrought iron tubes which form the rising mains or pump trees for the bore hole pumps. A certificate for £2,000 on account is submitted. Tar Contract—The existing contract with Messrs. J. Turner and Co. expires on the 30th prox. Instructions to ad- vertise for fresh tenders are required. Spent Oxide— We have in stock about 150 tons of spent oxide contain- ing from 50 to 60 per cent, of sulphur, which I would recommend be advertised for sale. Scrubber Washer— Some months ago Messrs. C. and W. Walker, the con- tractors for this machine, erected in 1889, applied, for the £5O which is still outstanding ; I declined, however, , to recommend payment, for although the work of the machine as regards the extraction of ammonia was satisfactory, the gear, which it will be remembered actuates the wood devices, was still most unsatisfactory, being frequently broken down and when working mak- ing a great noise and requiring too much steam to drive it. The contractors have since removed the gear com- plained of, and have at very considerable cost to them- selves substituted new gear specially designed to over- come the objections alluded to. As this is now working satisfactory, I beg to submit a certificate for the £5O balance of contract. Sulphate Plant—This plant has worked 10 days during the past month; four cwt. have been sold; present stock 10 tons. Water in stock July 27, 1892-9,264,939 gallons. The illuminating power of the gas during the month has averaged,l6.9B candles.— Recommended that the Clerk advertise for tenders for the purchase of gas tar for a period of 12 months; the purchase of the present stock of spent oxide; and the supply of about 25 tons of cast iren pipes.—The minutes were adopted.

div.head: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.
div.p: GENERAL PURPOSES COMMITTEE.

_ This Committee's report contained this item : Bower's Brook.—Letter, July 22nd, from the United Alkali Co., Ld., stating that they had received a letter from Mr. Stephenson, the engineer to the L. and N.W. By. Co., asking if they would do the work and stating the amount he considered it would cost, and that the Ity. Co. would pay them the amount, read and considered.

Mt. Midwood moved the adoption of the report, and referring to the item quoted, said Mr. Carey had waited upen the Railway Company and they had consented to let the Alkali Co. do the work at the cost of the former, and the work would be completed in the course of a month or two. The brook would then be in a better condition than it had ever been in. The Chairman remarked that that was very satisfac- tory for all concerned. Mr. Beck seconded the motion for adoption of the re- port, and it was confirmed. It was also resolved that the annual inspection of the Board's works be on the 25th inst.

A Liberal councillor named Taylor was the only candi- date legally nominated, and, on an appeal, the Educa- tion Department decided that Mr. Taylor constituted the School Board in his own person, and directed him sitting ,as the School Board, to fill up the four vacancies. This he will noir proceed to do. Sarah Castel! (49), married, was charged at Clerken- well Police Court, London, on Saturday, with destroying a list of Parliamentary voters exhibited outside the Hol- born Town Hall. Police Constable Shurrell said he saw the prisoner tear a leaf from the list of voters which was hanging from a notice board.. The prisoner said she thought the papers were put up for the public to take. She had no idea she was doing wrong. Mr. Bros ordered her to pay a nue of 10s.

div.head: FRODSHAN WATER SCHEME.
div.p: FRODSHAN WATER SCHEME.

The Locol Government Board wrote stating that be- fore s inctioning a loan for the execution of such a sblieme of water supply as that proposed for the town- ship of Frodshatn, they required to be furniahed with satisfactory evidence that a sufficient supply of whole- some water would ba obtained from the proposed bor- ing, and with a view to obtaining this information they would suggett that a trial boring should be made to the full depth proposed and that when the boring had been completed continuous pumping should be carried on day and night for a fortnight, and that the water be analysed. Messrs. Timmins, water engineers, Runcorn, submitted a tender to carry out the boring to a depth of 300 feet for £l5O and to make the observations re- quired by the Local Government Board for a further £55. This subject had been considered by the Frodsham Paro- chial Committees, who recommended that the tender of Messrs Timmins be accepted and that the sanction of the Local Government Board be obtained for the borrowing of £2so.—Mr. Williams in moving the adoption of the minutes, said this preliminary expense would form part of the original estimate of the schems. Mr. taron seconded the motioa, and stated Messrs. Timtnins's esti- mate was very reasonable indeed. APPLETON PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. Mr. John Whitlow proposed that is parochial Com- mittee be formed for the township of Appleton, and that the powers of the authority be delegated to such Committee, which should consist of the Guardians of the township, the ex-officio Guardians, and Messrs. Thomas Hall, D. L. Wright, James Tiusley, and Hugh Darby- shire.—Mr. Aaron seconded the motion, which was car- ried unanimously.

div.head: OUTBREAK OF SCARLET FEVER.
div.p: OUTBREAK OF SCARLET FEVER.

The Medical Officer reported that scarlet fever had occurred at Overton (one case),Hingswood (three cases). Kingsley (two cases), Acton Grange (one case), Preston ' Brook (one case), Preston-o'th-Hill (two cases), and Hat- ton (three cases). A case of typhoid fever had arisen at Sutton Weaver. The Medical Officer believed that in- fection in most of the cases had been conveyed through attending school.—A discussion ensued on the reading of the report, and the Medical Officer said children had been sent to school when suffering from the disease, and as some of the eases had.not been under medical super- vision, there had been no notification. The parents, or the persons in charge, were liable to a penalty for not notifying cases of infectious diseme, but they would not realise their responsibilities until a prosecution took place.—Mr. Stokes said this was a very serious matter, and something should be immediately done.—Mr.Brand- reth asked did the parents know that the children were suffering from scarlet fever.—The Medical Officer said there had been a serious outbreak at Warrington through a similar cause. Parents, in order to escape having to send their children to hospital, had not called in a medi- cal man or notified the outbreak of the disease until the cases hal become hopeless.—Mr. Brandreth asked could the doctor prove that the parents sent their child- ren to school at Daresbury knowing them to- be suffering from scarlet fever.—The Medical Officer : No, that is a diliculty.—Mr. Stokes said parents when they saw 1 symptoms of illness should keep their children at home. 1 —On the proposition of Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. Aaron, it was resolved to have placards printed, point- ing out to parents and others in charge of children the responsibility that rested upon them to notify to the Authority outbreaks of, Infectious disease.
SUTTON WELL.
The Inspector was instructed to take a sample of water from the well at Sutton.

div.head: HALTON BROOK SEWER.
div.p: HALTON BROOK SEWER.

The Inspector reported that a meeting of the Commit- tee to consider this matter recommended that the entire length of the sewer be piped under with 9 inch sanitary pipes and that the tender of Mr. Wm. Ashley be ac- cepted for the work.
NEW EfOI7SES.
A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. John Hedgcock for three houses erected by him at Stockton Heath.
ItUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present, Messrs. J. Knowles (vice-chairman), J. Stokes, T. Lea, J. Baguley, E. Aaron, T. Lewis, S. Taylor, E. Bretherton, J. M. Williams, J. W. Baguley J. Whitlow, J. Brandreth, J. Wilkinson; Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, J. Ashton (clerk). and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

div.head: DEATH OF MIS. ASFITON.
div.p: THE DEATH OF MIS. ASFITON.

The Chairman said before beginning the formal busi- ness of the Board he wished to refer to the great loss and deep affliction that had overtaken their respected clerk since the last meeting. Re was sure that he only expressed the feelings of every member of the Board when he stated how exceedingly deeply they all sympa- thised with him in the severe affliction that had over- taken him, and they trusted that that divine support would be extended to him which alone could afford him sufficient strength to bear his deep sorrow. (Hear, hear.) —The Clerk, who appeared too full of emotion for utterance, very briefly acknowledged the sympathetic remarks of the Chairman.
A SUBSCRIPTION.
It was resolved to subscribe two guineas a year to the Devonshire Hospital, Buxton, where a patient was to be sent.
THE COUNTY ASYLUM.

On the proposition of Mr. Tanner, seconded by Mr. Aaron, a committee consisting of Messrs. Williams, Taylor, the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, and the clerk (Mr. Ashton), was appointed to visit Chester County Asylum to inspect the lunatics from the Union.
REPAYMENT OF LOANS.

In accordance ;-vitb-a request from the Leytoustone Union, the Guardians resolved (on the motion of Mr. Williams, seconded by Mr. Knowles), to join with them in mmoralising the Local Government Board to extend the time for the repayment of loans for public works from 30 years to 60 years, as they did not see why Guardians should be placed in a less favourable position than Schcaol Boards, in respect of the repayment of loans required for the erection of buildings which in the mat- ter of durability are about equal. THE POOR RELIEF OF RUNCORN.-LIVELY DISCUSSION.

Mr. 2randreth said the Finance Committee recom- mended the payment of accounts amounting to £338 103. 3d, which included a cheque of £9O for relief at Runcorn, £3O for relief at Frodsham, and £l5 for tha pudworth District. At Fielsby they paid out Bs. 8.1. a week, and at Runcorn £3l 15s. 6:l.—Mr. Aaron : And how much does Runcorn pay in ?—Mr. Branareth : Not as much in comparison.—Mr. Aaron :—Let's have it.— Mr. Brandreth: Runcorn contribute £1,500 per year year to the Union and they take nut more t han £1,500 in their poor alone.—Mr. Taylor raid the £9O Mr. Bran- dreth spoke of included relief at Runcorn, Weston, Hal- ton and Ashton.—Mr.Bra.nclreth : It doesn't. (Laugh- ; ter.) He added that the amount from the whole of Run- corn relief district was £45 a week ; £3l was for Run- corn alone. To make a comparison £1,500 a year went to Rune°, n for outdoor relief, besides what poor were kept in the House. Helsby contributed to the Union £l6O a year, and they paid 6s. Bd. a week in outdoor relief.—Mr. Aaron : I don't understand Mr. Brandreth yet.—Mr. Wilkinson : But I do. (Laughter.)—Mr. Aaron : Does Mr. Brandreth mean the amount paid to the poor in Runcorn by the re- lieving officer for Runcorn.—The Chairman said this was a question which should be delegated to a small Committee to thrash it out.—Mr. Aaron persisted in questioning Mr. Brandreth. He asked what amount was paid in Runcorn alone.—Mr. Brandreth replied £3l 15s. —Mr. Aaron: And how much a week dos Runcorn pay in poor rates to the Union?—Mr. Brandreth : Of course that is another question.—Mr. Aaron: How much does Weston pay—why should you always be picking at Run- corn ?—Mr. Taylor : Because it pleases Mr. Brandreth and does me no harm.—(Laughter.)—Mr. Brandreth: I don't pick holes. Why Fam speaking about Runcorn is this, that there wants a Committee to go over these things. I move that a Committee consisting of the member for the township of Runcorn, and Messrs. Hey- wood, Brandreth, Peter Hall, Thomas Baxter, John Weir and William Whitlow be appointed.—The motion was seconded.—Mr. Taylor said the Runcorn Guar- dians had nothing to hide. They had endeavottied to be as careful as possible, and if this Committee could help them in guarding against imposition they would be glad.—Mr. Brandreth said there had been &great deal of money going out at Runcorn. There were cases in which 12s. 6d. a week was paid and had been for a. long time, and perhaps some of the children were 16 or 18 years of age and earning " good money." Be did not see that the relief lists of Runcorn were ticked by the members of the township the same as they were in the Frodshati district.—Mr. Aaron : I can't sit here and hear Mr. Brandreth tell bare faced palpable lies(loud cries of " order.") There was no order. For years and ondedinguya the G u quarterlyar. yearsmemeeting, n he nhda the never missed dians. div.head: ' HOLIDAY N OTES.-
div.p: ' HOLIDAY N OTES.-
BY TOUCH-AND-GO."

“Where shall we go for our holidazdy” is a ques- tion sometimes difficult te) decide ; 'out this year it was settled for me by learning. 'Sat an old friend and his family had made arrangements for spending a fortnight in the Lake District. I had "done the Lakes" mcrre than once,but to take the family there instead of to the seaside—and to have friends on the spot—Was a new idea. It was irresistibly tempting; and accounts for these notes being sent from Grange—not Grange-over-sands; but Grange amongst the mountains—Grange in Borrowdale.

"Change of air and scene" is a remedy one has heard of before when " a bit run down but it is none the worse for that. Let us have old friends, old books, and old remedies, when there is no doubt about their being safe and agreeable. 'And what a change it is from Warrington to Borrow- dale; from a flat country, smoke-smitten town, and sluggish dirty river to a land of mountain and valley, of fresh bracing air, and swift-running streams of virgin purity

But a word about Grange. It is not what is called under the licensing laws "a populous place ; for the houses of the village proper would all have to be told to reach the number of twenty. I see it from the window as I write— half a mile off—and what a charming picture it makes, with the gleaming Derwent bank full, the rich pasture land in the foreground, the low two- arched bridge spanning the river, the cluster of cottages just beyond, half hidden by trees, and the everlasting hills in the background suddenly but grandly closing in the scene. These hills form what are called " the jaws of Borrowdale," and Grange is by contrast a delicate morsel upon which, happily, these jaws have never yet closed.

From the 'window on the other side of the house we look down the vale, That broad sheet of water a little over a mile distant is Derwent- water, one of the loveliest lakes in a district where all the lakes are lovely. Looked at as a mirror, one must needs exclaim, after gazing on the well-wooded surrounding hills, What a beautiful frame it has !" And the charm of it is that mirror and frame are ever-changing. One hour they are bathed in sunlight; everything seems.sharp and clear; the hills thrust themselves upon you ; and the very trees have an individual asped. The hour passes, and the change is so great that you might be in another land. Alittle wbileago, Skiddaw, looking every inch his 3054 ft. blocked the valley at the other end of the lake and dominated the scene. But at this moment he has as completely disappeared, hidden by a cloud of mist, as if he had never been. And now even the lower hills are looking weird andstrange ; they assume new aspects even while you gaze, as if under the spell of an en- chanter. Mother nature is indeed a wizard and her tricks are inexhaustible.

One of the stories told of Borrowdale by way of illustrating the primitive simplicity of the inhabi- tants is given by Miss Harriet Martineau as follows:—" Spring being very charming in Bor- rowdale, and the sound of the cuckoo gladsome, the people determined to build a wall to keep in the cuckoo and make the spring last fox ever. So they built a wall across the entrance, at Grange. The plan did not answer, but that was, according to the popular belief, from generation to genera- tion, because the wall was not built one course higher. It is simply for want of a top course that 'in that wall that eternal spring does not reign in Borrowdale. "There is a similar legend attaching to a Yorkshire dale; but it has got such a hold up- on Borrowdale that it is ' insult to be wiped out with blood to call a native" cuckoo."

It was intended that Monday should be devoted to Keswick and climbing Skiddaw, after Sunday as a day of sauntering ; but it was a case of rain and rain and rain to it. At the first suggestion of a break in the weather, it was determined to have a row on the lake; hut by the time we had secured our boat and our man it rained harder than ever, although the younger members of the party made no account of it. Indeed, like ducks, they seemed to like it ; and so one hour was passed, and one island was rounded, and the shore was seen occasionally—as the mist permitted.

As if there had not been waterfall and to spare, it was next determined to see how the water came down at Lodore. ' Visitors who go with Southey's lines in their minds are usually disappointed; for except after or during heavy rain, there is n i oth- ing in the nature of a "rush and roar ;" it s simply a trickle down the rocks. We, however, saw the stream in full spate; and were delighted with a spectacle which, under the circumstances, was simply magnificent. Apart Altogether from the water, the gorge is one of the grandest in the lake district. The vast boulders—and they are vast—lie in confused heaps but in the most, "admired disorder ;" and Nature, in that delight in things lovely which she frequently manifests has beautified a scene, which would otherwise be crude and harsh, with moss and fern and lichen and tree. Cowper, a warm lover of nature, was indeed right when he said God made the country. and man made the town.

I had.intended to say something, of the outing next day to Buttermere ; butl time and tide and the Borrowdale postman wait for no man. The important personage just named delivers his letters as he goes up the valley ii the morning, and "picks up" as he comes down in the after- noon. He passes our ,domicile—Derwent View— about half-past four; but he is not like the hunts- man—he does not "cheerily wind his horn " ho whistles ' • and when he_whistles there must be no delay or the post is missed. Further reference therefore, to Buttermere, and how we got there, must be regarded as in the position of, Mahomed's coffin—suspended—for the present.

div.head: LANCASHIRE ASYLUM tOARD.
div.p: LANCASHIRE ASYLUM tOARD.
PROPOSED ASYLUM. AT WINWICK.
On Wednesday a meeting of the Lancashire Asylum Board was held at the County Offices, 'Preston, the Rev. C. T. Royds presiding. There was a full attend- ance of members.

The Chairman presented the report of the sub- committee on additional asylum accommodation. i here were, he said, three sites brought before the committee as combining all the requisites desirable for the proposed new asylum, any of which, he was sure, would meet the approval of the Lunacy Commissioners. The first site was uxbury Hall, near Chorley, containing 512 acres, and was offered in its entirety for £30,000, including the buildings. the timber to be taken at a valuation. If the estate were 'considered too large, the venders were prepared to sell them 330 acres and the building for £2OOO. The second site was Penwortham Priory, 1411 acres, at £lOO an acre, with a further 180 acres at £BO an acre; and the third was Winwick Hall, near Warrington, 130 acres, offered for £21,000, with so much more land as might be required at £l2O to-150 an acre, the timber to be taken at a valuation, and the minerals to be reserved. Witlyregard to available water this Site was within half a mile of the Warrington Water Works. The sub-committee had not expressed prefer- ence for any of the sites, as they were all equally eligible I—Answering a question, the Chairman said it was not considered desirable to erect Another asylum at Whi tting- ham, as there were already 2,000 lunatics there.—The Clerk read a letiter•from the clerk of the Liverpool Select Vestry, stating that the Rainhill Asylum was quite full, and asking the board to bear in mind the great number of cases sent from the Liverpool and West Derby dis- tricts. Mr. Houldingxoppported the suggestion that the new asylum be placed within reasonable distance of Liverpool.—lt was resotved, on the motion of Mr. J. Barrett, seconded by Mr. Rawcliffe, that the Committee ascertain and report the hest terms on which the Dux- bury Ball site could be obtained ; and a similar resolu- tion was adopted with regard to the Winwick estate, on thernotion o Mr, W. S. Barrett, seconded by Mr. J. H. Morgan.

To-day the united demonstration of Sunday Schools will take place at Widnes. There will be 14 schools re- presented, and about 3,500 scholars will be in the proces- sions. Proceedings commence at 2.30.

div.p: SUCCESS OF WIDNES BANDS.

At the brass band contest held-at Hindley. on Saturday the Widnes Subscription Band was awarded fourth prize; and Gossage's Soap Works Band carried off the filth prize. The well-known Platt Bridge Band-was one of the unsuccessful campetors.

RUNCORN POLICE News. At this Court on Thursday before Mr. Pl. Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Wig, George Holt was charged, under a warrant, with being in arrears on an ordm made against him in October last to pay his wife 15s. per week for her maintenance.—The woman said she had great diffi- culty in obtaining any contribution from the defendant, who, she alleged,spent large sums in drink.—The defend- ant promised to pay, the arrears at the rate of ss.a week, and the case was withdrawn.—Mary Tonke, Peter Walsh, and Samuel Tomlinson were each fined for drunkenness. THEFT OF A WATCR AND CRAIN AT RUNCORN.

A young man named Thomas Grant was brought before Mr. H: Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Wigg at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, charged with stealing a watch and chain, the property of Lucy Rawson, of 12, Hartley-st. The prisoner had been lodging with the prosecutrix for a forthight, and on Saturday last he went out and did not return. The watch and chain were subsequently missed and were discovered to have been pawned by the prisoner at Chester. He was anpre- hended at Wrexham and handed over to P.C. Wor h, of the Runcorn force.—The prisoner pleaded guilty,and was sentenced to a month's hard labour. - AN IRISH SPREE AT RUNCORN. Rose Higgins, lodging-house keeper, Mersey-at., was brought 'up at Runcorn Police Court on Thursday, charged with haying unlawfully and maliciously wounded a ship canal labourer, named James McGee. It appeared that the previous afternoon and evening the parties had been drinking together.—Superintendent Atherton described it as an " Irish spree" and about ten o'clOck a quarrel arose between McGee and the pri- soner's son, and they fought two "rounds "in the house. Whilst thus engaged it was alleged that the prisoner struck McGee on the head with either a jug or a basin, causing a wound which had to be afterwards stitched by Dr. McDougall. P.C. Lea was on the Scene immediately after the occurrence, and in his opinion the people were all drunk. The prosecutor was placed in the box, but it was impossible to get any information from hi m,as he said he did not remember anything about the matter. Under these circumstances the Bench dis- charged the prisoner. JOSEPH PRITCHARD'S sale shop Is 51,114 h-tit.. his workshop at Bridge-Bt.—Ada. \ ALLEGED CRUELTY TO HORSES AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Marshall Hughes, vanman to Mr. Walter Collier, grocer, Church- at., was summoned for cruelty to a horse by working the animal its an unfit state on the 23rd July. On that day the horse was drawing a van laden with bread, and - P.C. Ridgway found a raw wound about the size of a shilling on the off shoulder, under the collar. The horse was in pain, :Inspector Cooper corroborated, and said with the exception of the wound the horse was in good condition. The defence was that the horse had worn a pad until that morning, and the ostler had left it off be- cause be thought the wound was healed.—Mr. Collier confirmed this statement,and said the man had no right to leave the pad off.—The magistrates did not consider the case a serious one, and a fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was inflictad.—Joseph Cooke, Princess-st., labourer, was summoned for cruelly ill-treating a mare belonging to Mr. Sweetman, ccal dealer; Heath-road, on the Ist inst. It was stated that defendant was "in drink " and kicke.l the animal as it was being fetched from the field. The defence was a total denial of the charge.— After hearing the evidence,the Bench concluded that the defendant had kicked the horse in a sort of spree, and fined him 1311. and costs 15s. 6d.
OSEPH PRTTCHARD, Watchmaker and Seiveller, 51, High- -4,., and 4, Bridge-gt., Runcorn.—Adrt. SAD SUICIDE OF A YOUNG WOMAN AT HALEWOOD.

On Monday afternoon, before Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, an inquest was held at Hunt's Cross Hotel, touching the death of Esther Grace, of Halewo9d, whose body was found in a pit near Seeke on Friday evening. Mary Grace, widow, residing in Higher-road, Halewood, said the deceased, who was 23 years of age, was her , daughter, and unmarried. On Friday morning witness took her to Dr. O'llagan, of Garston, who told her that ' the deceased was enceinte. She had no idea of her daugh- ter's condition before that ; she took her to the doctor a-, she seemed unwell. Witness questioned the girl as to her condition, but she denied that anything improper had ever taken place with her ; however, later on in the day she admitted it. She did not seem distressecl.and witness did not scold her. Ann Grace, sister of the deceased, said the unfortunate girl left home about twenty minutes past two on Friday afternoon. She then seemed in her usual spirits. Matthew Sankey, labourer, said he saw the girl about half-past-two on the day in question, com- ing from her house and going in the direction of the place where she was found. 6She did not speak to him, but she seemed all right. P.C. Hardy (Spelre), deposed to recovering the body with grappling irons from a pit near Speke-road. The jury returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst in a state of temporary insanity." . .

A RUNCORN NRWZ.BOY'S ESCAPADE.

William Herringshaw, 13, was charged at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. H. Reynolds and L. 417igg, with stealing 12.. 2d., the moneys of Messrs. W. H. Smith and Son, of the bookstall, Runcorn Railway Station, on the 30th ult. Mr. Ebbrell, manager, stated that the boy had been in his employ about seven weeks. On the date named he was sent with papers to Weston Point,and ordered to collect the weekly accounts. Not returning, information was given to the police. On Sunday morning his bag was found on the canal bank, and the conclusion was arrived at that he had got into the water. The police dragged for him until late at night, when they received information that he had returned home. He told witness that he was counting his money when a navvy came up and took it from him. Iletried to regain possession when the man threw him into the canal. After he had sunk twiez a boatman rescued 'him. In answer to the question why he had not returned heine sooner, he said the state of his clothes was too bad. He entered the house without his boots, and stated that they were at Weston Point, but on the following morning they were found outside his home. When interrogated by Inspector Cooper, on Monday morning, he acknowledged that his previous statement was all lies, that he had taken the money, and that he had been to Liverpool, where he had spent it.—Superin- tendent Atherton said the boy was a crafty customer, ' and by his action caused Weston Point to be in a state of anxiety for him. The police, as well as a large num- , ber of people,dragged for him during the Sunday.—The , boy now acknowledged stealing us. 3d., and he was ordered to recieve ten strokes with the bireh rod, to be administered by Sergeant Woolley.

BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

From a return of the digest of endowed charities in the county of Chester' ,the particulars of which are not recorded in the general Digest of Endowed Charities in that county, which has recently been published, I find the name of Holy Trinity National School amongst the list of public charities. It is distinguished from some of the others by an aste- risk, which denotes the "possession of property unproductive of income (such as almshouses or school buildings) so'far as yet known to the Com- missioners.' This entry practically shows that Trinity School is endowed for the purposes,of edu- cation, and that the sanction of the Charity Com- missioners would have to be obtained before they could be put to any other purpose.

In the same list is brought to light the Anne Orred Charity, of Weston, which consists of £l,OlO 2s. Id., invested in new consols and other stock,and brings in an income of £27 15s. 4& per annum. The _ . 1--

incoine is stated to be distributed in money to the poor of the township. This charity was left by will dated 1847. Ido not remember the charity being referred to at the vestry meeting, but the distribu- tion'of so large a sum annually ought not to be overlooked.
The Eaton Charity of Halton is described as a fixed yearly paythant of .£7 Is. 2d., from real estate, half of which is spent on education, and the re- mainder distributectin money to the poor.

There was quite a little scene at the meeting of Runcorn Guardians on Tuesday last. It arose through a statement by Mr. Brandreth, chairman of the Finance Committee, to the effect that the whole of the contributions to the Union by Runcorn were distributed in out relief in that town; and he drew a comparison with Helsby • when the half-yearly payment to the Union was £l6O, and there was only distributed in out relief 6s. 6d. a week. There was no cause for a loss of temper over the subject.•lt should be remembered that two-thirds of the popu- lation of the Union resides within the limits of Rune.orn relief district, and that in the township of Runcorn itself, half of the population of the Union is to be found. And to make a comparison between such a populous district and a country village is ridiculous.

There are fewer paupers in the country because they are driven into the towns. Last census shows that while the town population is steadily increas- ing, there is no increase of dwellings in the country, and the population is steadily dimishing. The sur- plus population of the country come into the town in ssaich of employment, and- througt the keen Competition which goes on amongst all classes of unskilled labour, are compelled to live ,a band to mouth existence, and at the first breath of adver- Shy they are thrown on the rates. , Before the passing of the Union Chargeability Act in 1868, it was proved that the greater prepOrtion of the.pauper- isni Of town,was thus caused, and this was the reason for passing the Act. Previoue to that. time, each township was responsible for the cost of its own paupers, but the Union Chargeability Act caused a common fund to be criAited, so that those Who con- tributed the Paupers to the town should also bear their proportion of the cost when they became chargeable to the rates. Thereis nothing strange, therefore, in Mr. Brandreth's comparison. The jaw intends that such places as Helsby Shall pay its proportion to the pauperism of towns like Runcorn. But it would be much better if sufficient cottages were built in the country to accommodate the agricultural population, and if the land were so. manipulated that such populations would be able to earn a decent livOillood without flecking into the towns. Perhaps Mr. Brandreth will cease from what Mr. Aaron describes as " picking ,at Run- corn."

So far as, the cost of pauperi= per head on the 'population is concerned,the ituncornpnion compares favourably with other Che.hire .Union. In Run- corn Union the cost is Is. Oil., Altrinchatn, lid.; Birkenhead, Is. 21. ; Chester, Is. 81. ; Congleton, 1111. : Macclesfield, is. 3L; Nantwich, Is. 64d. ; North wich, Is. 2.1. : Slockport, 9d. ; Tarvin, 511.; and Wirral 9J.'
TERRIBLE ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.
TWO MES KILLED AND SIX INJURED.

• One of the most terrible catastrophes, that has ever taken place in Widnes, took place on Thursday afternoon;at what are commonly known as Hut- chinson's No. 2 works, Waterloo-road. *A large por- tion Of the works is being demolished by the United Alkali Co.,who have.s)ld the land to .M.e.ssrs.Gossage and Son for the extension of this firm's soap manu- factory. For twelve months the work of demolition has been going on, under the siiperinteu- deuce of Mr. A. G. Kyle, the eagineer, and this week a gang of men, working under a foreman. named john O'Brien, COI11:11tBle l•to pull down four large vitriol chambers. One was razed to the ground on qedne'sday without accident, an l on Thursday "O'Brieu's gang" stazted work on a second which measured ninety feet by sixty feet and about twenty feet high. For this purpose a powerful derrick was ' used, and precautions were taken to strengthen. the timbers so that they should Lot give way. About ' three o'clock the men removed some of the joists at the top of the framework, and also took away a tunnel which had been used to remove gas from one chamber to another. No sooner were the joists removed than the whole of the structure collapsed With a tremendous crash, and an adjoining caustid shed was buried in the ruins and destroyed. Luckily. there were no men I working in ,the shed or the catastrophe would have been even more serious than it. is.. Of the twelve mea who were engaged in the task of demolition ' four wereon the roof of the chamber, and they were thrown to the ground, but escaped with a severe shak- ing. Of three other then working on the Waterloo-road side one nanied Patrick Barrett, of Catherine.st.,jumped through au opening in the wall to the ground, a distance _ .

of twelve feet, and escaped uninjured, as did his com- panion, Wcsa. Rourke. At the side near No. 3 chamber • four men were at work, and on, hearing the creaking of timbers three rushed for a ladder at the other end,and having to pats odder the falling timbers, were burned lin the deb*. Two of them were killed, and the third, John Routledge. was terribly injured and his recovery is despaired of. The fourth man, %V. Connolly. of Pitt- . st., escaped by having the presence of mind to step it.to N 0.3 Chamber. Tha foreman was fortunate enough to ,be loaving the scene at the time. The inju zed men were immediately conveyed to the Accident Hospital, aii,l the wounds were attended to by the local doctors who arrived with great promptitude. The list of tlei kilted and injured is as follows : KiUed. Harry Srone, aged 45, married. 75; Ch rch-st. ; Dominic Kelly, aged '32, single, 24, Bridge-st. Injured, John - Routledge. Wright-st.l William Bruce, 51 Chohnondeley-st. ; Jos. Henegan, James-st. ; Thomas Foxley, Chnlmondriev-st. , Peter I.awton,3 Peel-st.-, and Peter Riley, 22 West Bank- st. Rontledge, who has a wife and numerous family, is fearftinv mangled and is not expected to,live. Foxley; it Mill 60 Fearfi•of age, is also in a critical state, having three ribs brol4en,and is very much cut and bruised. In the other CaSC.I3 the injuries are not serious. It is sup posed that since of the woodwork was decayed and that this haying given way, the chamber colLipsed.

The inquest on the bodies of the deceased yea i opened yesterday at Widnes Accident Hospital by Mr. S. Brig- house, County Coroner. Mr. 13..Farrant was foreman of the joky. The coroner said he had only come that day in order to take formal evidence of identification to enable the relatives of the deceased to bury them. He would then adjourn the inquiry to a future day. In answer to the Carotrr Sdperintendent Keighley said he would not 'be able to complete the inquiry without the evidence of the injured men, and he did not think any of them would be able to attend in a week.—After some discussion amongst the jurymen; it was decided to adjourn, until Friday, Angutt 26th, at 1.30 at Widnes Police Court.--Evidence of identification was then given by Mrs. Fanny Stone, widow of Henry Stone and Wni. Jeffreys, fellow lodger of Kelly. The jury were then bound over, and, accompanied by the Coroner, went to view the scene of the accident.

BANKRUPTCY OF A WARRINGTON MEI

At Warrington Bankruptcy Court, yesterday, Thomas Lawleo until lately a fish and game dealer in Corporation-st., Warrington, underwent an ex- amination in bankruptcy. In a statement which he had filed with the official receiver he said that his father, Wm. Law/ess, who had tarried on the business as a fishmonger and game dealer in War- rington, died intestate and insolvent on the 30th July, 1891. As administrator of his father's estate he carried on the business on behalf of the estate. Ilia father's creditors accepted and were duly paid a composition of 10... in the .e. In answer to the official Receiver. (Dir. Dibb), the bankrupt gave as the cause of failure bad trade and the large ex- penses he incurred in keepinz the family. He suc- ceede I to the business on the 30th July last year, so that he had been in business barely one year. Asked what. profit he had made out of his father's estate by the sett!ement of the estate he said lie had reCttflred only £lOO. The Official Receiver : I understand your father's estate yielded £2,398 ? . Yes.—The Officisi Receiver : And that includes £BOO advanced upon property to which you have succeeded as heir-at-law, I believe ? Yes.—The Official Receiver: Tell us what the property consists of ? It consists of an ice-house, curing house, stable, and yard at Heath Side. Warrington. I vaide that property at £l,2oo.—The Official Receiver : That repre- sents a difference of £4OO, which is one item of profit not brought into the account. You have saved £4OO by, the transaction-; you have also &wen the horses, carts. business utensils, house fittings, Lie. Yes.—The Official Receiver: What do you value those at? £so.—The Official Receiver: How many horses are there? Six.—The Official Receiver: Why they are worth more than £5O. Then there is also the furniture. Is it worth from £5O to £100? Yes.

In answer to further inquiries the bankrupt said be 11.1 d had to maintain five brothers and five sister.; be i .43; himself. They were working for him, and he paid them separate wages. The expenses of keeping the t ainily set down at £5 a week. In addition to this he paid two of them 10s. a week, one 45., one 25., and one is. 6d. and another person ss. Altogether it cost to n.aintain the family about £6 103. . . . . .

The officialßeceiver : The whole of that has come out of your creditors. You have not made one singlel sixpence as profit justifying the payment of that £6 103. a week. Did you take any steps to ascertain whether you were justified in withdrawing that amount every week P—l thought that trade might get better. , —He added that he had not kept proper books. He first ascertained that ha wes working at a loss about Christmas.—The Official Receiver : Do you say deliber- ately that since Christmas you have been carrying on that business knowing you were taking out of you: creditors' pockets something like £6 I.os. a week? Is that what you mean to convey to the court? Yes.—Do you wish to justify this in any way, or have you any excuse to offer? I thought trade would mend.—The Official Receiver After satisfying the mortgagees, your defici- ency will be £325. In the short twelve months you have been carrying on business you have managed to , make away with something like £725. lam not takingl into account the furniture or horses, but there is £4OO from the property and £325 deficiency, that is £725. We want you to explain where this has gone to, apart from the £250 or £3OO spent in keeping the family ? I had the old men to keep.—The Official Receiver : Why were you keeping them ? I took over my father's business,and they were working for Jilin. The Official Receiver next asked the bankrupts if he knew .what gross profit he had made. He admitted that env answer he made would be a guess, upon which the Official Receiver re:narked that it was not worth while wasting time on that. He added that since Christmas he bad contracted debts with the knowledge that he Icould not pay them, unless business mended. He had not filed his petition before because he was in hopes that business would mend Plnd that he might by cutting off expenses work the business in a different way. He had not the :lightest idea what his turn over Was in the week. Be had kept no cash book and not a single record of money received or paid away. lie had I carried on the business in the sania way as his father eatrieds it m. The Official Receiver said lie should require a clearer account as to where the £7OO had gone to. The bankrupt was also questioned by Mr. Unsworth and others on behalf of creditors. He said that he had had a turn-over of between £5O and £6;./ a week. He had lost nothing by betting, although he had betted in small sums. The highest bet he had ever made VMS Ifor ss.

ALLEGED BIGAMY.—At Frodsham Police Court,on Tues- day, Alice Halcroft, alias Alice Hughes, was charged under warrant, with having committed bigamy, by marrying John Efughes, navvy, of Frodshani, at Overton Church, on th Bth September, 1890,her husband Edward Haleroft,being then alive.—Halcroft stated that he mar- ried the prisoner at Govilen, near Abergavenny, on the 23rd December, 1873, and the prisoner was remanded until Tuesday next. THE MASHONALAND MISSION.—On Sunday evening the Right Rev, the Bishop ot Mashonaland (Dr. 0. W. H. Knight Bruce), till recently Bishop of Bicemfontein, in South Africa, preached in the Parish Church, Frodsham, the offertories being in aid of the above mission.of svhich Dr. Knight Bruce is the leader and founder. Mashona- I land is in Southern Africa, and although little known hitherto, has features of exceptional interest. It lies between the northern border of the Transvaal and the Zambesi, bordering to the east on the Inaian Ocean, and to the west on the land of a great nation known as the Matabele. The total offertories amounted to ES Is. sd. There was not such a large congregation as had been ex- pected, owing to the very heavy rains. WOUNDING i DAUGHTER-IN-Law.—Peter Jones, (55) labourer of Frodsham Bridge, was brought before Mr. A. Thomas and Dr. Steele at Frodsham Police Court on Tuesday charged with unlawfully wounding his daugh- ter-in-law Mary Butters on the 30th July, with intent to do her grevious bodily harm. The prosecutrix stated that on the night of the date named she went into the pri....mers house and her mother-in-law asked her to lend her VI I. Witness asked " Won't h- give yo,, 10. and Mrs. Jones replied •• No." The prisoner who had been in the garden came in during the conversatt in. with a shovel in his hands, and with this he st ruck Mrs. But- ters on the back of the he4d causitna a large woand. He afterwards threw he- out of the house and kicked her. few minutes later P.C. Weatherby arrived on theacene and being a member of the Ambulance Corps he band- aged the woman's head with her apron and then sent for Dr: Burton, who ordered her to bed and kept her , there several days The Doctor informed the magistrate that the wound was an inch and a half long, and almost ' penetrated to the bone. There were several small, arteries cot which had to be tied. When apprehended by F. C. Weatherby the prisoner said "I have not done it." Ho was committed to the Quarter Sessions for trial. Suitors ASSAULT ON A WOMAN.--YeSterday at Frod- sham Police Court, Wm. Siddley was charged cn remand with having on Tuesday morning, attempted to com- mit a rape on Alice Cooper, a stranger, on Chester main road, at Dunham The woman stated that on the previous night she went into the Rtilwa.v Hotel, and the prisoner afterwards entered atal aske I I her to have a drink and she had a glass of beer. she tald him that she was going to Chester to see her sister. When she left he followed her and after going some distance and in a lonely part of the road lie seized hold of her by the throat, but was prevented fr.nn effecting his purpose by the intervention of Joseph Ball, a game- keeper, who was in an adjoining•field.—The prisoner was afterwards apprehended by P.C. Manley. He was again remanded for a week.

The forces of the Sultan of ,Mordeco on Wednesday advanced against the Angherites, whose villages can be scen from Tangier. The result of the day's fighting, was disastrous to the Imperial forces, who were driven back with considerable loss. The cholera riots at the Persian town of Astrabad and the attacks on Russian subjects have been followed by the lauding of a Russian force of infantry and cavalry on Persian territory from gun boats on the Caspian. The Cossacks were promptly sent to Astrabad to protect Russian subjects. The report of this invasion of Persian territory is rightly described at Teheran as of serious importance. The cholera is increasing at Teheran.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
Al' WARRINGTON.

I observe that preparations are being made in the - Park for the erection of the new band stand. Ido fervently hope that it will far surpass its ugly pre- • decessor, which was a decided eyesore—though it must be said that the music dispensed from it was the reverse of an earsore, and was calculated to make one quite forget the place from which it emanated.

I hear that in consequence of a rumour that a batch of new magistrates were to be put upon the bench in Warrington, some well-known members , of the Tory party have been in a state of sup- pressed—or, rather unsuppressed—excitement for a few days past. They have been enlarging upon their personal claims with an extraordinary amount of candour. But the peculiarity of the situation is this, that while these modest gentlemen trumpet their own virtues, every other Tory one meets speaks of their own qualifications with the utmost derision,

There is a possibility of Winwick Hall being turned into a lunatic asylum, and, indeed, the Lan- cashire Asylum Board have already gone so far as to instruct a eomtnittee to ascertain the best terms upon which the estate can be purchased. The in- habitants of Winwick, speaking generally, are not elated at the prospect; in fact, some of them talk as though they didn't want an asylum any nearer to them than Rainhill. " What we want at Winwick Hall," said an intelligent resident of the ancient village to me the other day, "is a gentleman with about £4,000 a year. But then," he added,and there was just a touch of melancholy in his voice, "no- body with £4,000 a year is going to live there." " How is that ?" I queried, as I had always been under the impression that Winwick was an emi- pently eligible place for a person of means to Ike at. " Well, you see, every time he drove to War- rington he would have to go through those stinks from Longford depot." I told him that we bad it on good authority in Warrington that the odorous smells were a pure myth, but. he was obdurate. He had smelt them, and that was enough for him.

A clerical speaker at the recent anniversary dinner at the Clergy Daughters School said he felt ' that the duty of proposing the toast of" The town and trade of Warrington was a heavy burden, because he understood that there was not a trade unrepresented in the town. His informant had ' certainly somewhat exaggerated Warrington's com- mercial comprehensiveness, but some day the boast may become well founded, for its trades keep ever and ever increasing. I cut the following item from a weekly paper, which is an instance in point : A steel wire railway carriage seating, made by a t Warrington firm, is, it is said, fast taking the place of the padded and volute spring seats. The new seat is composed of minute steel wire rings com- pactly knit together, over which only a very thino layer of hair or a pad of felt is necessary. The Lon- t' don and North-Western Railway has already fitted 653 to their carriage and saloon berths, while the - Great Eastern Railway has in use nearly 5,000.

It has frequently been predicted that our national sports cricket and football would ultimately be driven out of existence through their gradual de- cadence in consequence of their becoming so much ,• identified with betting. Warrington is pre- eminently a football town, and it will be un- pleasant news to it to learn that what was predicted as to football is absolutely being realised as to the American national game of base ball. The Boston U.S. "Beacon" says that it, as a manly sport, is slowly but surely passing into a state of innocuous desuetude, and remarks that the disbandment of.: the great professional clubs in the near future may ' be looked for, adding "The sport has lost its c:larm ;. it has become a scramble for many, a gambling scheme, and a nuisance generally."

I have been much struck by the fact that most of those cases of female rowdyism which have ef late so disgraced the streets of Warrington and indeed' adjacent districts have proceeded from quarrels about politics. It is certainly a new phase in political life when this element instead of the usual domestic tittle tattle or scandal is beginning to excite so much fierce interest among the female viragoes who are so numerous in our midst. We read of a recent case in the district, in which the hanging out of a window of a red petticoat in indi- cation of the political complexion of the owner produced upon the women of the contrary side of politics in the neighbourhood the effect which a red rag does upon a bull, and occasioned a perfect convulsion among them. On the recent', election day in Warrington, it was commonly said that the women made considerably more noise than. - the men; and I myself saw some extraordinary scenes of what I might fairly call political delirium among women,which perfectly staggered me. What , a delightful thing it would be if these clamorous. females would take to reading the newspapers, and' discussing politics in the streets with acumen and discrimination! There would, indeed, be a change,. I have heard Methodists say the greatest swearers become he most fervent prayers when converted. Perhaps by the same analogy these same obstreper- ous females might become the most formidable.. bench women, I will not say for the Primrose Dame,: but for the dame of the Women's Liberal Associa— tion, if they could become chastened by a little more political culture. But all! this is too much to dream of.
MERLIN.

div.p: WAD. RINUrTON LICENSED VICTUALLER • ASSOCIATION.

The members of this Association,together with a. few friends, held their annual picnic on Thursday,. and the place the Committee agreed to visit on this occasion was " Osmaston Manor," the Derbyshire seat of Sir Andrew Barclay Walker, subjsct, of course, to their obtaining the consent of Sir Andrew - to do so.

The Secretary (Mr. P. Brimelow) communicated the desire of the Committee to Sir Andrew, and lie gener-;' ously replied that the Association and his permission t,. visit the Manor, and,moreover, expressed the hope that the gathering would partake of luncheon whilst they were- there. The kindness thus expresged was readily accepted, and as a result about one hundred and! twenty ladies and gentlemen assembled on Thursday' morning to enjoy the outing. Accordingly at 7.50 a.m. the party took temporary possession of five saloon -carriages, which had been arranged for at the Central Station, and, running into the Manchester Central Station, were connected with the London Express, and after a very pleasant and enjoyable run arrived at Derby: Awaiting the arrival of the party here were a number ok. conveyances of various designs and shapes, but all equipped in the very best manner, the " horse- flesh "eliciting the'• admiration of all concerned., Driving from tke station, a short stay was made at the County Hotel. Presently all was again on' the move, and good progress was made from Derby to Osmaston, a distance of about 12 miles. Here the party were met by Mr. Turner, and, dividing themselves in two, one party made a tour of the gardens, greenhouses, and portion of the grounds, whilst the other made a survey of the interior of the house. At the conclusion of this it was announced that "luncheon was ready" whereupon the united party made their way to the Racquet Court, for the time being converted into an extensive dinner saloon, where a sumptuous luncheon was laid. Two AD'
7S Y01T1113.-AEMED WITH A LOADED PISTOL.

At the Warrington borough police court,on Wednesday morning,John Smith and William Smith, bays, of Sankey Bridges, were charge.] with being hiund sleeping on the premises of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co., and being without visible means of subsistence, early that morning.— A constable deposed to finding the lads on the premises, and that John Smith had upon him 4d. and some pistol caps, and William in his pockets a pistol fully loaded, about half a lb. of powder, and about half a lb. of shot. He said his mother gave him a sovereign on Monday morning to go a message, but instead of going home, he bought the pistol far 25., and the powder and shot. He had 7s. Bd. left, which he had given the watchman at the works.—The watch- man corroborated this last statement, and said he had taken the money from the lad at the request of the father, who worked at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co.'s, and had handed it over to the father.—The Chief Constable said in that case there was no offence. —The Chairman (Councillor James Fairclotigh) said as money was found upon one of the lads, the charge of having no visible means of subsistence could not be proceeded with.—The mother of the lad said she did not send them out with a sovereign, but it was stated they had been sent out for beer.—The Chair- man : Children have no right to go for beer, to get into bad ways.—The Chief Constable : Perhaps it would be better to hand him over to the county police to prefer a charge against hirn of stealing the sovereign.—The pri- soners were disaharged.

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. S. 11. Armitage.

CHARGES OF TriFFT.—John Brian was charged with stealing £1 123. 9d., the money of David Evans, at Haydock, between the 16th and 17th July. From the evidence adduced it appeared that the prisoner had lodged with the prosecutor for about five or six weeks. On Saturday, the 16ch ult., about eleven p.m.,prosecutor saw the money safe in a drawer on the sideboard. He locked the drawer up, and he and his wife went to bed. The prisoner, who had possession of the front door key, had not come home, and his supper was left on the table. The next morning, about seven o'clock, the pro- secutor got up, and on looking about the house,he found several articles of clothing belonging to the prisoner. In the kitchen lie found the prisoner's gold ring on the window-sill, and his suspicions being aroused, he went to tbe drawer, and found that the money had been ab- stracted. He afterwards went to the prisoner's bedroom, and found he was missing, but the bed had the appear- ance of having been slept in. Information was given to the oolice, and prisoner was eventually apprehended by P.C. Davies. In reply to the charge of stealing the money he said, " I have taken none of their tnoney." He was remanded until Newton Petty Sessions.

div.head: SEVERE EARTHQUAKE IN GERMANY.
div.p: SEVERE EARTHQUAKE IN GERMANY.

A.severe shock of earthquake; lasting ten seconds ,was felt at Ems, Coblenz, Valender, Nassau, and Neider Lahenctein at half-past eight on Wednesday morning. The disturbance was accompanied by loud subterranean rumblings resembling thunder. At Nieder Lahnstein the (=illation was so great that chimneys fell and a school building was damaged. A panic watl created in a school at Coblenz, and the pupils rushed terror-stricken into the roadway. At Ems many houses were shaken, and the shock was so severe that the visitors who were bath- ing left the baths.

div.head: COTTON' OPERATIVES AND THEIR WAGES.
div.p: COTTON' OPERATIVES AND THEIR WAGES.

The proposal to reduce the wages of the operative engaged in the cotton trade continues to arouse much comment throughout the county. At Preston Bury, and in many other towns the suggestion has been made that the best method of checking over-production would be to establish a working week of forty-eight hours, really an eight-hour day, and a general ballot is to be taken on the question. At Bolton the idea prevails in some quartrrs that it would be well to extend the August holiday in preference to either a reduction of wages or the institution of the eight-hour system.

At West London Police Court, on Friday, John Jen- ner, a greengrocer in Kensington, was fined £2O and £3 3s. as costs, with the alternative of two_ months imprisonment, for having caused a giandered horse to be led or driven along a public highway. John Morgan, publican, and Annie Norton, a young woman, were tried at Bristol Assizes on Friday, for throwing vitriol into letter-boxe-s. The woman was further tried for attempting to set fire to the letter box and for setting fire to tiw dwelling-house of John Lovell. Several postmen in different parts of the city, found that the letter-boxes had been tampered with, by the in- troduction of either sulphuric acid or nitric acid. This had burnt the contents. .

_ The steamship Hartville, bound for Greece, ran into the fishing smack Telephone, of Ramsgate, off the North Foreland, in the night. Out of the three hands two were drowned. The captain was saved, and 'orougli,t t. Dover on Friday morning.

WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.—This return match was played at Wigan, on Saturday, and Warrington again displayed inconsistent form, Wigan reversing their de- feat of a fortnight ago, winning on the present occasion by a large majority. It was to be regretted that neither of the Crosfields was able to play, whilst R. Smith was also absent, for Wigan had mustered up a strong com- bination. including R. G. Barlow, the old county pro- fessional, and T. Ainscough, an old Wigan player, but I now located at Ormskirk. Captain Manson won the toss, and sent in George Clarke and J. A. Yonge to face Barlow and Goodwin. The former's third ball Yonge played on, and Manson dame. Runs came but slowly, and then by the aid of singles until, at 18, Manson failed to get hold of one from Goodwin. With two wickets down for 18, Warrington's prospects looked eloomy ; but disaster did not end here, for Bell, after getting Barlow away twice to the boundary, was bowled I at 28. Clarke had meanwhile displayed extraordin- ary patience for FO hard a hitter, but with Voisey's dismissal he was tempted to hit out II at Barlow, and, from a skier, he was caught at the wicket. Three wickets fell at 31, and in an hour andl ten minutes the whole side rare dismissed for the miserable score of 41. Wigan started none too well, as Rennick, W. Wall, and Barlow were all out at 18, but pn H. Wall and Ainecough being associated, runs were piled on at a rapid pace, fours being frequently sig- nalled. Woods took the ball from Bell ten runs after the Warrington total had been passed, but the partnership had realised 84 runs and the total 80 before Wall was c and bby Woods, his share being 30. Twelve runs later Macauley was sent back, but some hard hitting, coupled with loose fielding, augmented the score at a rapid rate. All interest was centred on Ainseough reaching his cen- tury, which he did after batting two hours and a half, having helped to take the total from 14 to 292. The worn-out bowling was severely treated by Hammersley and Murphy, and the end came, no doubt as a relief for Warrington,with Wigan's score as 303 for eight wickets. The fielding of Warrington was far below the average. Score :

div.head: SHOCKING DISCOVERY.
div.p: A SHOCKING DISCOVERY.

A horrible discovery was made on Sunday evening near Althoy p Railway Station, the headless and armless body of a woman being discovered in a sack, secreted in a ditch by the side of the main road from Southamp- ton to Rugby. The head and arms had been cut off by a person possessing some anatomical knowledge. The clothing indicated, that the victim was not of the poorer classes. The linen was fine and well made. The police are making ingoiries„ but at present, they know noth- ing, except that no woman in the country is known to be missing. The road where the body was found is very seclude.d,and tntirely screened from observation. It is suggrsted that the body was brought by train from a distance, and was carried by a man on his shoulders to the place where it was found, and where it had been lying undisturbed for at least a month possibly two or three months.
A full suit of clothes, including a stove-pipe hat, has reached the house of a certain new member of Parlia- ment, whose "make-up" is just now attracting a great deal of attention at Westminster.

NOTES ON GAMES AND
MISCELLANNOus. _ _

At the Star Inn Race Grounds, Si". Helen*, on Satur- day, about 2,000 persons assembled to witnese a foot- race between James Heesom and George Cook, both of St. Helens, for £l5 a-side and the championship of St. Helens. A very good race resulted in. Heesom winning by half a yarti; The distance was lUoiyards.

At the Athlone sports held in connection with the Hats, Ringway, nd Ashley Floral and Horticaltoral Society, on Saturday, J. S. Haynes, a promising War- rington runner, managed, after a hard race, to bring away the first prh'e in the half mile fiat race handicap (open),.

The man Peat, who won a heat in the 100iyards event at Warrington Footbalt Club sports, and was objected to by Webster, turns out to be a professional, named Heesom, of St. Helens,who won a match for All against Cooke, of St. Helens, ors Saturday. Some will also remember The fact of a man named Stockton being turned away from the starting post in the maiden race. It has since been learnt that be was a Manchester pro- fessional residing at HarpurNey. The pistol fireroMr. E. Kane, recognized him, and promptly ordered him,off the ground.

Several Warrington cyclists managed to pull off a number of prizes at the Manchester Wheelers Sporbs,the proceeds og which were in aid'of the Manchester Ware- housemen and Clerks' Orphan School. In the mile novice ,bicycte race, T. Hope, of Warrington, carried off the third prize starting fram the *yards mark. Sutcliffe, Manchester Wheelers, 30 yards was first ; Seddon, Manchester• Wheelers, 30, was second;, and J. Miller, Manchester Wheelers, 40, fourth. The race was a good one, a half yard dividing the first mid second ; four, the second and third, and one third and fourth. Time,.. 2mlns. 421 sec. Hollins Allen won the second heat in the. half mile bicycle handicap, with 35 /yards in the favour,, but his name appeared not amongst the final winners. In the two miles inter-club race Warrington took third place with 123 points. Manchester C.C.. were first with 6, Manchester Wheelers being second with the same numbev. Oreenheyes and Longsight also ran a dead heat with 19 points, Manchester C.C. being 60 with 24. The Warrington men came in •as follows :-Ist heat, Rollins Allen, 3; second heat, J. Buxton, 3; third heat, W. H.. Bellian, 3; 4th heat, T. Hope, 5---At the Stock- port Cricket Club Sports on Saturday,. H. Rowe, War- rington won the first prize, having '4O yards start.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

Referring to the Lancashire v. Yorkshire match the "Manchester Guardian "says, "The state of the score when stumps were drawn on the Monday established, we believe, a record for first-class county' matches. We have dht been able to discover another instance in which a county team scored 437 in an afternoon. The score was also, we are inclined to believe, a record for the Lancashire Eleven although it has been exceeded by the "Gentlemen of Eleven, on more than one occasion. In July, 1.867 the Gentlemen of Lancashire scored at Old Trafford 586-.rons against the Gentlemen of Yorkshire, Mr. E. R. Rowley contributing 219 and Mr. Whittaker 146. In 1874 the same sides being engaged, the Lan- cashire Gentlemen made 525, towards which Mr. Ilernby contributed El? and Mr. A. R. Rowley 944 Bp his innings of 1801 Albert Ward very closely approached the Lancashire County record, which is held by G. J. Ricketts with the fine score of 195, made at the Oval in June, 1867, the total in that innings being 429. A great deal was expected of Ricketts after that phenomenal dis- play, but he disappointed the county by his subsequent Orformances: Mr. Bright said of some of the landed gentry : "They came over with the Conqueror, and never did anything else." So Ricketts, at that memor- able battle on the oval, came suddenly into great pro- minence, but immediately subsided, and was thencefor- ward only a very moderate performer."

Some of the Yorkshire papers are reviving the old controversy as to the "birth qualification " for county players, and it isoiuted out that in the matches played last week the men who were most prominent were not playing by right of birth., Thus, Nottingham owed a 1 large portion of its success against Surrey to Shaokloa, a Derbyshire man, Surrey was immensely indebted to Lockwood, a Nottingham man ; and Lancashire's champ, pions against Yorkshire were Ward, of Yorkshire, and 1 Smith and Briggs, of Notts. With regard to Ward and 1 Lockwood, Lancashire and Surrey are clearly entitled to the credit of having appreciated their fine qualities and, given them opportunities for distinction; and Briggs.' learnt all he knows- of cricket in Manchester. The Surrey Committee would probably be the last to propose that only the birth qualification should entitle a man to play, for a county. The enforcement of such a rule would: deprive them at once of Lohtuann, Sharpe' and Lock- wood, and possibly of others. Nottingham, too, would have to' part with Piir.Dixon (who is a Lincolnshire man) and Shacklock, and" Lancashire and Middlesex would be literally annihilated.

Shrewsbury's scores in the Kent match raised his aggregate above the coveted thousands, and he will probably end the season with a far better record than his last year's aggregate of 794 in county matches and 1;071 in all matches, If the great Nottinghs m batsman would once and for ever abandon the only part of his " method " to which* objection can be taken he woald be perfect, hut until the /aw of leg-before-wicket is altered he is, of course, justified in defending the stumps with his legs.

The Lancashire fast bowler, Mold, just before being engaged for the county of Northampton, was, it is said, played for the small, provincial town of Banbury. HO. bowled there with deadly effect; and many a well decked Oxford University man (with his college honours fresh upon him) found himself obliged to suc- cumb ignominiously to the terrible pace and sweeping spin of an unknown nountry-town bowler.

With regard to batting averages, W. W. Read has dropped from the fourth to the sixth place, and with the exception of J. Shuter and Read (M.), the remainder of the Surrey team found that Notts match was a kind of refrigerator for their figures. It made them contracts. Ward (il.) has comeagain. and now holds the seventh position with 34.12it0 his credit ; his nearest county col- league being Sugg, in the sixteenth hole wits 252.' Briggs has made a big jump, but he is still a long way behind Baker ; while a fairish distance exists before the next Lancashire man, S. M. Crosfield, is reached. W. G. Grace has improved his position from nineteenth to thirteenth, and nocv has the respectable figures of 27'16 to his name.

Wainwright, with 32.95, looms a long way ahead of the rest of the YOrkshire contingent, even if we include F. S. Jackson, whose average is 22.95. Sellers and Lord Hawke are.eompanions with 1900. and 18.79 'res- pectively, while trlyett looks wistfully after, his nobte captain with his 17.46 figures. G. Bra.nn's fine innings the other day gave him a helping hand, as it wereto climb over a boss of notable crieketers, and getinta the top half of the table.

Several counby matches were brought to a Conclusioai on Wednesday. At Nottingham the home eleven were I set to get about a hundred runs to defeat Middlesex.,and I they accomplished the task with the loss of two wickets. I The play was dreary in the extreme, the Notts batsmen I suddenly develt.ping to an extraordinary degree their characteristic style of "stonewalling." Mr. O'Brien asked Mr. Scott to bowl a few overs, and at last himself tossed the bait to the natsmen, in the hope that they would get the necessary nnmber of runs and bring. the "game" to ran end. A conclusion was reached at last, to the relief of fielders and spectators. In the match at Brighton Yhrkshire defeated Sussex by nine wickets. Probably the best cricket of the day was seen at Ilirken• head, where Cheshire defeated Leicestershire by five runs. There was a brisk attack and a vigorous defence in the la&t half hour, and both tearrA deserV.o great credit.

div.head: FoomAIL.
div.p: FoomAIL.

TheLancnOldre Rugby League an accomplished fact at last. It will not be known by that name, but "a rose by any other name would smell as sweet," and, Under the title of the Lancashire Challenge Cup com- betition, all the beauties of a league will be.sem and the fragrance enjoyed. Notonly will the advantageg of a league be 'enjoyed by the select few, but., under the comprehensive scheme proposed by the county, every club affiliated to the Lancashire Union, will be alare to participate in a competition having all ' the peculiar advuatages which leagues are supposed.to*possess.

Thisvital step was tailten at a meeting of representa- tives of the County, and was called by the members on the clubs which have been so active and so assiduous in promoting a League. for Lancashire. It is historical 'matter now that the failure to convince the Rugby .rnion that a League was necessary to Lancashire was not due so much to,the want a argument, but rather to the unfortunate fact that a " rebellious body" from Yorkshire wal appealing at the same time for permis- sion to form an &Rance. This.was fatal to both coun- ties, and Lancashire had to saffer for Yprkshire's indis- cretion.

But while the Torkshireme4 were acting antagonisti- cally ta their-- immediate govZrning powers, the Lanca- shire group received every encouragement from the Palatine Committee, and though the Rugby Union had to tar botila applications with the same brush, individual membeas of that august body were singularly in sym- pathy with the Lancashire men, and thoso holding high authority in the COMIC:HS of the Union advised Lanea- shire to promote some scheme whereby they could have the. competition without coming into opposition with the Union's ruling.

Hence, with this ,Autspoken opinion to animate them, it is no wonder that the Lancashire County Committee resolved to take such steps as would give effect to the aspirations of the pubs who were clamouring for a League, and on Friday, alter the committee had pa- tiently heard Messrs. Murray and Mason state their case

for the projectors, Mr. Payne proposed 'that a Challenge Cup coninetition be instituted in Lancashire, and that the scoring be according to the mode adopted by Leagues—that is, by points, after every club In the com- petition has met every other c.ub. The proposition was seconded by the chairman (Mr. Grover) sad passed un- animously.

The purchase money to be paid for their ground by the Bradford Club is £13,000. Half of this sum ,has been paid down, and the remainder has to be paid for at the rate of £5OO every half year, without interest, until the whole is paid off. According to this agreement it will be nearly seven years before the, purchase is paid for. The club has also to pay the Bradford Corporation £l,OOO for road compensation; and with other expenses the buying of the property will total up to a formidable job.

The memory of one of V9arrington's sons will now, says the "Athletic Newt," be perpetuated as long as graven monuments resist the ravages of tune, for during the past week a handsome memorial stone has been erecSed over the last resting-place of T. Jolley, the well- known footballer and csicketer. This tribute to his memory has been subscribed to by ail his admirers—and they are many—and now a magnificent monument, embellished with symbols or the games be loved, marks the spot where Jolley sleeps the sleep. that knows no waking. It is a beautiful testimony of the esteem in which he was held, and it is a credit to his native town.

It is stated that the Notts COnimittee are so pleased with the performances of their men that it has been resolved to entertain them at a banquet, to which the public will bo admitted. This monition was arrived at before Gunn and Barnes had made such a fine stand "in the gloamin' " on Tuesday evening.

A RACIAL RIOT IN AMERICA...

Naw Tani, TBURSDAY.—A telegram from Yessup, Gsorgis, states that a riot is in progress there, and that both whites and negroes are armed and ready for blood- shed. Troops have been sent to the scene, and many are said to have been shot. Further details are want- ing.

div.p: THE WEST HAM MYSTERIk..

At West Ham on Thursday, George Herbert Bush, twenty-three years of age, labourer, was again brought upcharged on his own confession with the murder of Amelia. Jeffs, by administering poison to her at West Hann in 1890. The evidence showed that Busbhad suf- fered terms of imprisonment, and had.beenconfined in tvsa asylums. The magistrate said that on the evidence and dates before him it was impossible for Bush to have committed the crime, and he was acossdingly dis- charged.

div.head: PITTSBURG IRON TRADE. WORK TO BE RESUMED:.
div.p: THE PITTSBURG IRON TRADE. WORK TO BE RESUMED:.

PITTSBURG, THURSDAL—The differences between the ron manufacturers and the Amalgamated lfion and Steel Workers' Association have been amicably settled by mutual concessions, and the threatened strike of iron- workers here and in the West has thus been averted. Fifteen of the Pittsburg mills will resume work at once. and others will do so as soon as the repairs now in pro- gress have been completed. While the settlement directly affects 25,000 to 30,000 rkilled workmen of the amalgamated association, fully MOM other men are interested in the result. The Homestead strike is not affected irk a direct man- lier by this settlement, inasmuch as .Messrs. Carnegie and Co. did not take part in the conference.
