SPORTS OP ISM:Wilt—lt is not generally known that some of the smallest insects are discovered to enjoy themselves in sports and amusements, after their ordinary toils, or satiating themselves with . !sea, just as regularly as is the case with many numan beings. They run races, wrestle with each ,?ther, and, out of fun, carry each other on their . sada much in the same manner as boys. ,These Pleasing characteristics of insects are particulerly 'e observable among ants, which are remarkable for 'their sagacity. Bonnet, a French author, says he leserved a small species of ants, which, in the inter- 'Arals of their industry, employed themselves in carry- each other on their backs, the rider holding with 4111 mandibles the neck of his bearer, and embracing it closely with. his legs. Gould, another writer, on e tuns, mentions that he has often witnessed these 'eeZercises, and says, that in all cases, after being oar- . Tied a certain length, the ant was let go in a friendly . Manner, and received no personal injury. This amusement is often repeated, particularly among the sal ants, who are very fond of this sportive exercise. ' It was amongst the same species that Huber observed similar proceedings, which he has described with his usual minuteness. "I approached," he says, "One day, to the formicary of wood ants, exposed to the sun, Mad sheltered- from the north. The ants Were heaped upon one another in great numbers, and appeared to enjoy the temperature on the stir- face of the nest. None of them were at work; and the immense multitude of insects presented the appearance of a liquid in the state of ebullition, upon which the eye could scarcely be fixed without difficulty ' • but when I examined the conduct of 4 each ant,l saw them approach one another, moving their antennm with astonishing rapidity, wile they Patted, with a slight movement, the nheeks of other ants. After these preliminary gestures, which re- sembled caressing, they were observed to raise them- selves upright on their hind legs by pairs, struggle together, seize each other by a mandible, foot. or antenme, and then immediately relax their held to recommence the attack. They astened upon each Other's shoulders, or bellies, embraced and overthrew each other, then raised themselves by turns, taking their revenge without producing any serious mis- chief. They did not spurt out, their venom as in their combats, nor retain their opponents with that Obstinacy which we observe in their real quarrels."

RULES OF GOOD BREEDING.—A German prince, L Who has recently published his Tour through Great v Britain, informs us that the three following are the : greatest offences which any one can commit against English manners :—" To put his knife to his month : instead of his fork; to take up sugar or asparagus ' 'with his fingers; or, above all, to spit anywhere in k A a room. These are certainly laudable prohibitions, , and well-bred people of all countries avoid such Practices-though even on these points manners alter greatly; for Marshal Richelieu , detected an adventurer, who passed himself off for a man of • rank, by the single circumstance of his taking up Olives with .his fork, and not with his fingers. The ridiculous thing is the amazing importance which is , here attached to them. The last-named crime is so I Pedantically proscribed in England that you might i; .ceek through all London in vain to find such a piece t• of furniture as a spitting-box. .A Dutchman, who Was very uncomfortable for the want of one, de- dared, with great indignation, that an Englishman's only spitting-box was his stomach. These things' are, I repeat, more than trivial; but the most im- P9rtant rules of behaviour. in foreign countries

almost always regard trivialities. Had I-, for example, to give a few universal rules to a young traveller, I should seriously counsel him thus : In Naples, treat ,the people brutally; in Rome, be natural ; in Aus- tria, don't talk politics ; in France, give yourself no airs; in Germany, a great many; and in England, don't spit. With these rules the young man would get on very well." OBEERVANON OF FOREIGN COUNTRIES.—There to not a single branch of science which does not require some labour and attention; there is not even O mechanical art to which some apprenticeship is not necessary. No naturalist would visit the Alps With a view to examine the structure of the globe, unless he had devoted some time and study to every object which conld mature his judgment, and give vi‘lidity to his opinions. Yet persons who have Passed their lives with books, who have seen human nature in print, or who have not seen it at all, go to distant nations, and describe as universal truths . . .

What they perceive there, under impressions arising from inexperience and astonishment. The usual feeling upon first visiting a foreign country is Prise, the the natural attendant upon novelty; and the Sentiment is shared not only by the vulgar, but by the enlightened: It is accompanied by pain or Pleasure, as the objects seen are in discord or In harmony with the disposition of the observer; but in either case it is generally exaggerated. Every day diminishes the impression, till at length the Customs which astonished inexperience are looked upon with as little wonder as those which were left at home. But no condition of mind is more hostile tn calm observation than a state of emotion which magnifies and disfigures truth. On the other hand, again, when habit, which has the power of destroy- ing sensibility to peculiar customs, has diminished the perception of things worthy of attention, much IThicb, when new, excited astonishment, no longer 0. attracts observation.—Chenevies Essay/ on National Character. COUNTESS or OntrNEY.—The following curious anecdote is related of Mary Countess of Orkney, Man died some years ago aged 76 :—She was deaf ;411t1 dumb, and was married in 1753, by signs. She lived with her husband, who was also her first cousin, at his seat, Ilostellan, on the harbour of Cork. Shortly after the birth of her first child— : th, e lady is lately deceased—the nurse, with con- . alderable astonishment, saw the mother cautiously PProach the cradle in which the infant was sleep- 10g, evidently full of some deep design. The tonntess having perfectly assured herself that the Child really slept, took out a large stone, which she had concealed under her shawl, and to the horror of the nurse—who, like all persons of the lower order in her country, indeed in most countries, was 'allY impressed with an idea of the peculiar cunning tlti malignity of " dumbies "—raised it with an Intent to fling it down vehemently. Before the arse could interpose, the countess had flung the ; not, however, as the servant had appre- elided, at the child, but on the floor, where of course it made a great noise. The child inamedi- relY awoke, and cried. The countess, who had onked with maternal eagerness to the result of her ;zperiment, fell on her knees in a transport of joy. nhe had discovered that her child possessed the "ense which was wanting in herself. She exhibited to many other occasions similar proofs of intelligence, tit none so interestin;. div.head: FEELING THE BUMPS.
div.p: FEELING THE BUMPS.

It was the hardware trade which ha cl onie en- gaged the earnest attention of Mr,. Andrew Griggs; and so greatly did it thrive under his auspices that he was enabled while yet in his prime to retire into private life with a handsomebalance at his banker's, and some decent-looking thousands in the Funds. His retirement, however, was not particularly private after all • for being of an unidle spirit and commendably well disposed toward his fellow-men, he encouraged his philanthropic ifid soon began to take an actiye part in the local affairs of that Midland' dounty borough where he'made and spent his money. Another person who showed a great interest in the same local affairs was a Miss Judith Bootle of no trade, but of a put-you-all-to-rights occupation. She was generally regarded as a strung-minded, woman, and fairly justified her reputation by actually owning to thirty-live years of age—only a slight extenuation of the true facts of the case; and as a member of the School Board, ratepayer, visitor to the workhouse, patreness of a soup kitchen, share- holder in the Ga,s . and Water Works, and 'Lady Vice-President of the General Reform Committee, she, managed to keep her name pretty prominently, before the public. That Mr. Griggs and Miss Bootle should fre- quently come in contaet was but a natural result of their respective functions ; and it became a matter of common observation that if ' there , was any- body who could soften the prejudices. or subdue the opposition of Miss Bootle, that body was Mr. Griggs. One day it so happened that Miss llootle called upon Mr. Griggs o,t his house, and in his official capacity of vestryman. He politely asked her to sit, down, which she did, and then; without any beating about the bush, propounded an alternative scheme for an eitension of the sewers, made inquiry as to the expense of some: recent municipal festivities, and complained seriously of the manner in which the new road-paving was being done. Mr. Griggshad . long been wishing to give the Ray a little bit of quiet'advice, and thinkfng this a favour- able opportunity, he waited' till 'she' had finished talking, when he thus began: "I hope you will not take it unkindly of use, madam, for saying what I' am going to ; but are not these matters rather outside your proper sphere ? " " I really don't, see that they are," rejoined Miss Bootle decidedly. "As nobody else will take them up, I suppose I must." • ' "Hardly so, I think," answered he, highly con- scious that he was treading upon delicate ground. "Now, in such things as attending to the wants of the poor and the education of children your assistance is most appropriate and extremely ser- • viceable." , "Thanks much !" said she. "But when, it oomes to mixing yoarself up with' municipal questions which 'have always,been con- sidered the peculiar province of men—" ' "Au, that's just how we poor women are always being crushed ! " interjected Miss Bootle.. "Nobody wishes to crush you, I hope," said the gentleman gallantly; "and what is more, I'm sure they couldn't if they would." The lady replied to this compliment by a smile and a bend of the head, which seemed to admit that the expression she had used was perhaps a little too rhetorical. .

Mr. Griggs proceeded in a mollifying tone, ".But it appears to me, my dear madam, a great mistake for any lady who is favourably known for her public spirit to overdo it. Look, for instance, at my good friend, Mrs. Crunch. What admirable public work she has done in this town for years past ! Yet she never dreams of interfering with— with vestry matters for instance." ' "You must recollect, Mr. Griggs, thg she has had the advantage of a husband—" "An advantage, I presume, which Miss Bootle might easily have enjoyed herself had she chosen." "Excuse me, Mr. Griggs, but is not—ahem !—is not this matter rather outside your proper shere And having propounded this question, Miss Bootle held up her head triumphantly, evidently consider- ing that she had scored one. But Mr. Griggs was equal to the occasion. "Perhaps lam a specially interested party," said he, with an arch look.

"Well, whether you are or not, I don't mind tell- ing you that the right sort of husbands aren't so plentiful that they can be picked up any day." "It won't do to be too particular," was the rather bold reply. • "Many thanks for the advice," said the lady in a mock-scornful tone. "When I meet with a good sensible man, 'one I feel I could look up • to, and whose sound iudgment I could rely upon, why, then perhaps r may—" "What would you say to me, then ?" asked Mr. Griggs, half jokingly. He was getting excited. ' Miss Bootle laughed. "I should jump at you, of course," said she, "provided you really behaved like a sensible man, and didn't go down on your knees or any stuff of that sort." Then she laughed again, and then they both laughed; and then he perceiving that the conver- sation had reached a dangerous pitch, thought it better to adjourn the meeting. So he told her that he couldn't wait, in consequence of having just recollected that he had an appointment elsewhere, and she just recollected that she had another, and they promptly said "Good morning, "and he bowed her out at the front door.' Here it may be as well to give some further description of these two individuals. Mr. Griggs had no personal appearance; Miss Bootle bad a great deal. Mr. Griggs was neither .tall nor short; he was neither dark nor fair, ; none of his features asserted themselves; he wore whiskers, I believe, very likely no moustache, and very likely beard; his dress was so plain yon couldn't notice it; you might have see him to-morrow ond never recognize him. On the other hand, there was no mistaking Miss Bootle—she looked very philanthropical. She had an erect figure; her features though strongly marked, were comely; and her expression would have been fairly feminine had she not more than counterbalanced it by a masculine style of outfit. Her brown hair was cropped short, and surmounted by a billycock hat; she wore a white stand-up collar, and a silk necktie with a horseshoe pin in it; her jacket was made as much like a double. breasted Chesterfield overcoat as possible ; her laced boots were high at the top and stout in the soles; and she carried a walking-stick. Unsym. pathetic persons thought Judith looked very "'nanny ;" Andrew thought that she looked rather nice; but then they regarded her from different points of view. When Mr. Griggs reflected upon the peculiar in- terview above mentioned, a thought came into hi- head---and it had been a casual visitor there before —that he might do worse than take Judith Bootle unto himself for a wife. Would she have him! Didn't she say she would jump at him? There was many a true word spoken in a jest ; and so on and so forth, until, by a process of seasoning which may be easily imagined, he arrived at the conclusion that quite the best thing he could do would be to pro- pose at the earliest opportunity. Their tastes were very similar, excepting, perhaps, in the matter of costume, and that might be quickly toned down; she was not at all unpleasing m his sight, and of a suitable age for him ; and indeed he had but one misgiving, which was that she might perhaps prove just a leetle too strong-minded. The fact was, Mr. Griggs did not feel altogether confident of his ability to• rule such a wife as Miss Bootle was likely to prove; and having an amiableipreference for being at the head of his own house, he did not fancy the prospect of being reduced to the position of Number i Two n the said establishment. • Permeated by this matrimonial problem, he was walking abstractedly down the street, when ho became aware of a pale head looking out at him from a shop-window, and then he became further aware that the head was in sad want of a wig, while the pate was very much cracked, and seemed to be covered with many little slips of sticking:plaister. Arousing himself from his reverie, he began to investigate the matter more closely, and found that the head was in reality a phrenological bust placed there as the trade sign of that most distinguished phrenologist, Professor J. Octavius Wagglesworth. Mr. Griggs stared for some minutes at this eccentric article, and had carefully read all the names of the various human qualities that were inscribed upon the slips of plaister, when a brilliant idea struck him, and, like a man of energy, he acted upon it at once. Entering the shop, he closed the door behind him, and then emote with his umbrella upon the floor. , .
"Professor Wagglesw—orth within 1"

div.head: THEIR FIRST QUARREL
div.p: THEIR FIRST QUARREL

The dpor slammed berween them, sate on the inside, and Harry on the outside; for they had just had their first 4arrel—a real, genuine, bona tido quarrel, and it would be hard to say which one felt worst about it.

." To think that Harry should have refused me the first thing I ever asked of him I—the very first. Oh, what humiliation! I feel ready to vow that it shall be not only the first, but the last thing I shall ever, ever ask of him. Oh 1 oh ! oh!"

And then tears and sobs came so quick that the young wife couldn't find breath for words to make that rAsli vow. By and bye Mrs. Katie, haviug cried away her bad temper, began to feel very much ashamed of it; and all at once she felt her- seq to have been very unreasonable in having asked th 3 best and most indulgent husband in the whole world to buy her a certain set of turquoise ornaments when she knew be could scarcely afford it, and had met with some rather troublesome business losses in the course of the past six months. "To think I should have quarrelled with Harry, and about such a thing What must he think of me? Oh I how ashamed lam But I'll say so the very minute I see him. I'm not above owning my faults' thank goodness. I'm not quite so bad as that. And now what shall Ido to show how sorry lam? AI:, I know? I'll make those shirts lierry was eking about. I'll make them with my own hands and the assistance of a sewing machine, and Harry will be awfully pleased, for, it is an accomplishment to be able to make a shirt." .- . And in a few seconds Mrs. Monolair was cutting out the shirts, basting them together, and singing meriiiy to the accompanying cheerful hum of the sewing machine. Meantime Harry Montclair had quite recovered from the momentary irritation that had forced his first impatient words from him toward his pretty and charming little wife. "My precious little Katie! What a bear 'she must think me," he said to himself, about the middle of the afternoon. lie had received dis- patches and letters by which he learned that certain recent ventures promised to be very profitable; and that already he was richer ,by several. hundre pounds than he had supposed himself to be that morning. "Dear little Katie should have the set of turquoise, ithe had to go without cigars for a year." It must have been about two hours later that Mrs. Montolair became aware that all the people in the vicinity seerned to be suddenly taken with a fancy to hurry past her house, and there was a strange appearance of haste and agitation about the crowd. "0, ma'am !" exclaimed one of the servants who bad been hanging over the gate for news, "there', been an accident—a frightful accident ?" "What kind of an accident, Nelly ?" asked Mrs. Montclair, catching her breath. "The ferry-boat, ma'am—an explosion—the boiler I" gasped the girl, as she caught her half- fainting mistress. "But don't give way so—per- haps the master wasn't on the boat." Katie made a desperate effort for composure, and asked in a hoarse, steady voice : "Do you know what hour it was ?" "Four o'clock, ma'am ; but, sure, Mr. Montclair doesn't raways come on that boat."

- "You know he has never once missed it, Nelly —never! Oh, merciful Heaven! What shall I do! What shall I-do!", .... . ~ Her knees seemed to sink under her, and every drop of blood seemed-to -roth back on her heart, then to rush madly through her veins to her head; and, with a smothered cry of anguish, she burst from the girl's restraining hold, joined the hurrying throng, and flew madly onward toward the boat-landing. There, perhaps, she could learn the truth; and perhaps it was only a false report, 'anyway. It must be! It must be! Nothing so awful could be true. The heart refuses to believe calamity, even when the reason sees it clearly; and already Katie Montclair felt the terrible news was true. There had, indeed, been a fearful accident; and soon—too soon—the report was con- firmed. It was a fact, a horrible, blood-curdling fact, and no power on earth could make it otherwise. The surging crowd were soon at the boat-landing, straining their gaze across the wide bay to the landing on the other side; but it was quite impossible to see anything. But over and over again Katie heard repeated all there was to know. The four o'clock boat had but just started on her trip when a terrible roar was heard of the explod- ing boiler, and the unhappy passengers were, in a moment, all face to face with death, and struggling at fearful odds with that dread enemy. "Perhaps our friends were not on board," said one and another; and "perhaps Harry was not on board," thought Katie, as she heard similar words spoken all around her. Then came another telegram, the contents of 1 which were almost instantly known to the anxious, waiting crowd, and the news spread as the wind blew. The less of life was terrific, and already boats were picking up dead and living by scores. Groans and shrieks went up from the waiting crowd; women dropped, fainting to the ground, and were dragged away by strangers from the trampling feet, unheeding or uncaring where they stepped. Katie Montclair was stifling with anxiety, crushed and despairing, but unconscious of her own danger, when, she suddenly heard her name called, and felt a telegram thrust into her hand. The messenger boys had taken this means of de- livering the messages intrusted to them, lightly guessing that the greater number of those to whom telegrams had been sent would be found standing about, waiting for news.. Poor Katie never knew how she did it, but in an instant the yellow envelope was torn open, and her wild eyes had devoured the words: "Missed the four boat. Home soon. Don't be alarmed. HARRY." Then she fained, and would have fallen hut for a friendly hackman who recognised her, and pick- ; lug up the unconscious form, placed her in a car- riage, and drove her home safely to the care of 1 her anxious servants. But again and again she I read over the brief message of hope and life, and her tears flowed for the many poor hearts to whom no such cheering words had come, or would come forever. It was late evening when Harry Montclair at last arrived,,,and clasped his sobbing • little wife to his heart. 1 "Oh, Harry, Hariy, forgive me! I will never ,be so unreasonable again. Let our first q,narrel be our last," she pleaded, penitently. • "Don't think of it, my 'darling," said Harry, trying to calm and re-assure her, though almost as much agitated as herself. "Who knows,—per- haps that quarrel saved my life, because I went up 7. town to buy this set of turquoise, and that was how I missed the boat. Look, dear !" and opening tbe case, he displayed the coveted j, webs. "Oh let me never see them !" sobbed Katie. "To think I should have quarelled with you about a necklace I " "But they saved my life, Katie—" " Ah, well, of course I shall love them always if they even helped to do that," said Kattie. "But, no, dearest, it was God gave you back to me, little as I deserved such kindness, when so many other poor women will never sec their dearest ones again. But, ah I perhaps they had not parted in anger. That was the bitterest thought of all, dear Harry, that I had been cross. I wouldn't say, 'Good-bye.' I pushed you away when you stopped to kiss me. .That thought was almost worse than the dread of never seeing you again. But Heaven is good. I have you now, and never, never shall I let you leave me again with an angry feeling in my heart. 1 If I had lost you, Harry, that thought would have I burned in my brain till the last hour of my life. Promise never to quarrel with me again, Harry— never, never 1" . , "Never, my own little Katie," said her husband, solemnly; and Mend her aga,l4__ __ _

div.head: Etttero to the Obitor.
div.p: Etttero to the Obitor.
TII E PUBLICAN'S MANIFESTO.

Sir,—ln letters at least six inches long Bung calls on Working-men" to strike for freedom—and drink— Sunday drink, and concludes his manifesto in large letters, with a wild shriek for " Liberty for ever." Free- dom to fuddle and Liberty to lush! What did the judge say at Liverpool a few days since ? It was that there was" no greater enemy to liberty than the pub- lic-house, no greater foe to freedom than the public- bause." Freedom and liberty and the public-house are the extreme opposities of each other ; men barter away their freedom and liberty there. A sixpenny pie and a quart of beer for a penny, and if we get our man in something extra, this is the Ardwick mode of working for a candidate—and this is liberty, this is the boasted freedomto buy votes. A blue barrel of beer on a hand- cart rolled to and fro in Hazel Grove on the election day so that all on sundry may drink success to the blue candidates. This is liberty with a vengaace.. I

Why is Bung so solicitous and show such tender anxiety for the poor man's comfort, that he should make such frantic attempts to give him his Sunday glass of beer? Is it pure benevolence—unadulterated philanthropy—that causes all this excitement that he should rush into print of such enormous dimensions. No, sir, it is not the working-man, the poor man's comfort that he is so anxious about—it is the poor man's pocket he wants to get at. There may be something left from Saturday night which it would be well to secure en Sunday. By the clatter and hum that you hear when pass- ing a. public-house on Sunday tromone o'clock to half-past two, you would suppose that the majority inside had had more than one class, and if the poor man is there he is where he ought not to be, for if he is poor he has no money for driak. Bung is not for short hours of work—no eight hours day for him. Other tradesmen open at eight and close at seven or eight at night, a half holiday in the week, and shut all day on Sunday. Bung has 17 hours every day and wants Sunday as well—to give the "poor man his glass of beer." His anxietiy for the poor man would be quite refreshing if it was disinterested—but it is not —it is the poor man's money he hankers after. If I could not live by six days honest work without encroach- ing on the seventh, I should think it was time to lie down and die. I want the seventh for rest, to recoup the body after from 54 to 60 hours toil, to replenish the mind so as to keep the intellect at par if not at a pre- mium, and without drink. . . . .

The trade and its supporters say that the Welsh Sun- day Closing Act is a failure. Eeither they know nothing about it, or they are wilfully false. My own experience and that of others who reside in South Wales, in the great seaport of Cardiff and Swansea, say it is a decided success. A policeman in Swansea told me he had been three years in the force and had never seen a drunken person on Sunday in all that time. There was trouble at Cardiff six years ago with bogus cluLs and sheheen shops but that is stamped out. Let us then have Sun- day Closiug and sobriety—local option and the suppres- sion of the drink shop wherever it is a nuisance ; let those who can protect those who cannot protect them selves—helpless wives and defenceless children. lam Sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. Sankey Bridges, August Bth, 1892.

div.head: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.
div.p: LIFEBOAT SATURDAY.

Sir,—To all who are interested in the lifeboat cause, the letters written by Lady Roscoe and Mrs. Macara will be welcome, and with your permission I would like to make a suggestion. I, with many others, have read Mr. B. G. M'Connell's letter of the 27th ult. wherein he makes a suggestion for the creoperation of a ladies corn- mittee. It is evident that this portion of his letter has attracted her ladyship's and Mrs. Macara's attention, and it is to be sincerely hoped that their letters Will 6timulate others to join in this great work of raising funds for the maintenance of one of Eng- land's noblest institutions. As one who, previous to Mr. Macara's appeal of last year, took no active part in this work, and who since that time has had special opportunities of witnessing the great in- terest which all classes take in this movement, I am convinced that the claims of the institution need only placing in a clear manner before the public of this country to ensure a permanent annual income sufficient for its requirements. I would therefore suggest that a council, to be called the " Lancashire Lifeboat Satur- day Ladies' Council" be formed consisting of 30 or 40 ladies from Manchester, Liverpool, Stockport, Black- burn, Oldham, Preston, Bolton, and other towns, the object of the council being to establish in each towns "Lifeboat Saturday," and 1 would eventually go fur- I ther and establish in each county throughout the coun- try a ladies' council to be named after their respective I counties. The ladies' cour cil could then elect a com- mittee in each of their respective localities who would solicit small annual subscriptions from their friends and residents, each member of the council occupyings. the position of president over the committee in his own district. If, also, in addition collection books were placed in the bands of children I am certain it would result in many hundreds of pounds being sub- scribed towards the fund ; and if the committee be once thoroughly organised, there will be found many helpers, ready to assist forward this movement to a successful issue. As an instance of the sympathy of the British public with the lifeboat men, one needs only to refer to the report of the " Liverpool Courier" respecting the imposing demonstration and pathetic incidents shown at Liverpool on Sunday week on the occasion of the funeral of the three gallant lifeboat men who lost their lives in the storm of Tuesday, the 19,h ult., and who counted life not dear unto themselves, so that they might save others—" It is calculated that the mournful proceedings were witnessed by about 200,000 persons. The public was everywhere most sympathetic and orderly. The sad event had evidently taken a firm hold on the hearts of the people and one practical outcome of this was, that many of the poorer working classes paid a visit to the Town Hall, prior to witness- ing the funeral, in order to place in Use Mayor's box their mites towards the relief of the large and young families left by the three men. A pathetic and unusual incident occurred. An old woman, very poorly clad, weeping pitaously, was seen to fall on her knees as the procession approached, and she continued in this attitude, praying until the last carriage had gone past." If Lady Roscoe will only undertake to carry out the formation of a council and Executive Committee, there are many gentlemen connected with the Saturday Life-boat Com- mittee, who would gladly render her ladyship every assistance in the preliminary work connected therewith. Your readers will be glad to learn that this movement is making rapid progress in many important centres of the country.—Yours, &c., Manchester, August 5, 1892.
ONE TO THE RESCUE.

SOCIETY. • On Weduesday, the 11th inst., this society had their spring bird race from Worcester, 84 miles. Mr. Durnbell the club convoyer, took charge of eight baskets contain- ing 220 birds on Tuesday, and proceeded by 11.58 p.m. train (Central) -to Worcester, the raw point. Wednes- day being fine, the, birds were liberated simultaneously at 8.55 a.m., wind north. The toss was witnessed by Mr. I. Collins, convoyer to the Liverpool Flying Club. The first bird timed in arrived at 11.8 ,• a few minutes over two hours in 'doing the distance: It cannot be known until velocities are worked out who are actually win- ners.

Some o' th' gentry 'll gad th' remainder o' th' Aristocracy to tek a less royalty on every booarder they introduce, an' at last they'll come deawn varra low i' their teims, sooa as to compete wi' firms like Cook's an' Gaze's; for there'll be some o' them Boort knockin reawnd, offerin' three weeks' halladay "in- cluding a week's board at Marlborough House" for twenty guineas. Ov coourse yo' find yo'r own bac- carat ceawnters.

Well, aw'm beawn to be thi' fost on th' job at knobstickin', iv th' aristocracy do ged mad at me. Hear yo'. To parties abeawt to booard th' Aristocracy. Heaw to save nineteen hunderd a year an' learn twice as mich. Turn o' Dick o' Bobs hes a tooathri vacancies for ladies an' gents wantin' introductions. Terms a bunderd a year. Bankers an' other refer- ences required. T. o' D. o' Bobs lies th' followin' specialities on eggsibition : . . . .
gtervin' childer7fro three month awd uppards, Drunken men an' wimmen, o' ages; Balaclava heroes i' various stages o' destitution ; Widows an' orphans o' deceased life boatmen. An' other choice lots."
Neaw then, yo vacant booarders, come early an' bring yo'r characters wi' yo' ; clergymen accommo- dated too.

Aw could intloduce the paysons to a interestin' case. It's a lad as werkt at Smith's book stall at Runcorn, an' a fortneet sin' he were sent to collect some brass, an' he did'no come back, th' poleece were put on th' job, an' they fun th' lad's bag o' papers aside o'th' cut, sooa they naturally con- cluded" he were drowned. It's an owd dodge,but them chaps naturally would conclude sooa; they dragged th' cut to no porpus for th' lad torned up at hooam th' same neet. Ile said he'd bin robbed bi a navvy, an' chuckt in an' rescued after he sunk twice, but he owned up to th' Inspector as he'd bin to Liverpool an' spent th' brass he'd collected. Re- ward, ten strokes wi' th' birch rod. Yet Smith an Sons sell lots o' books wi' nod half as mich in 'em; they mek a lot o' brass eawt on 'em, an' sooa do th' chaps as write 'em, but this lad as may ha' read an' acted up to 'em—well, id is herd lines !

Juries are very fond o' bringin' in verdicts o' "temporary insanity," an' that's abeawt th' com- monest way they hey o' showin' their ignerance o' human nature. They were at id agean last Mon- de' at Macclesfield, at a inquest on th' body ov a young actor as shot hissel theere. In a letter to th' manager o' th' company he were wi' he said: " Last night ... an old complaint ot my eyes came once more over me. On a previous occasion I had to relinquish my employment for ever—l was a draughtsman then—and my sight was useless to me for some time. Not chosing this time to be- come a burden to my relatives, also being some- what tired of life, and having no fear for anything hereafter, I have in the full possession of my rea- son, and after carefully studying the question on all sides decided on the step lam about to take."

He gooas on to say wiieere th' balance of his salary is for nis landlady, hooaps th' authorities 'II provide him wi' a" wooden box," and says: "1 am resting under the fond hope that my few relatives, with whom I seldom communicate, may not hear of this. . . . (I am having my breakfast as I write this—curious, isn't it)." _

Everything considered aw think poor Nosworthy were as sane as th' creawner an' jury ; an' he's nod th' fost suicide be mony a theawsand as hes bin. When a chap hesn'd a friend i' th' wide world, an' feels i' th' way o' everybody, an' knows there's nobbut a revolver bullet, or a p.nn'oth o' pizen, be- tween him au' rest id seems to me a natural thing to tek to. Even Judas lied sense and pluck enough to goof& to suicide to end his agony. Eli, it's a grand thing to hey a friend!

Wod do yo' think abeawt 'em hevin' a observa- tory on top o' Mont Blanc? Heaw's thad for heigh ? Aw dorn'd expect we shall hey ony better weather for id, though we may hey moore deeaths bi accident, through fooak tryin' to reych th' place. Id wodn'd be a bad idea to plant thad big tallyscope up t'neere—aw meean th' new un as is beawn to lick th' Lick instryment, an' shew us things on th' moon iv they're th' size ov a factory, id'll be a staggerer iv we find villa residences theere tenanted fri, gentry as " tek in" lodgers—but aw herdly think they'll be thad civilized. Aw'll tell yo' ov another good idea as struck me when aw were readin' perlymentary news t'other day, an' th' dry rot as were tawkt : pass-eatot checks ! Heaw's id strike yo'?.

There's nobbut one moore parragraft th' noos- pappers as hes med mi meawth watter this week, an' that's abeawt Johannesberg bein' built on gowd; aw've read o'er London bein' paved wi' gowd, but bein' built on gowd caps me. " Gold reefs occur in almost every part of the country," say the Times correspondent, an' when yo' come to read o' th' increased eawtput every year yo' realize as id mon be sooa ; for th' fost hofe year (1887) id were 23,155 eawnce, an' then id went up wi' a run, this rooad : _

1888 1889 1890 1891 For th' fost six month o' this year it's moore nor 562 theawsand eawnce ! That's wi' poor machinery, an' one white mon i' every ten. An' yet, fooak atop i' England to be werkt to deeath for a bare livin' ; werk at th' forge sixty heawra a week at thrippence an heawr, an' when they ged tired o' thad they emigrate to places wheere they're no use. Iv aw were a strong young chap wi' no encum- brance aw wodn'd be long afoore aw were i' th' Transvaal; an' when aw'd med mi pile aw'd come hooam, an'—ha, ha, ha '—aw'd gooa an' hey hofe a year's booard wi' a Duke at forty peawnd a week An' iv aw couldn'd ged some Brimstoon an' Traycle for ml brass—well, pappers as think o' geddin' a special Commissioner on th' job 'll happen please N .B.

div.head: DAMAGES AGAINST THE L .B.ND N. W. RAILWAY COMPANY.
div.p: DAMAGES AGAINST THE L .B.ND N. W. RAILWAY COMPANY.

At the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Williams, Mr. Charles Allcard, surveyor, of Tue- brook, sought to recover from the London and North- Western Railway Company damages for personal injuries to his wife. She " missed her footing "at night on the staircase at Tuebrook station, and broke her leg. It was alleged that the Company's servants turned out the lamps just as she was putting her foot on the first step. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, with £lOO damages.

div.head: CHESTER "PAUPER" WORTH £7OO.
div.p: A CHESTER "PAUPER" WORTH £7OO.

An extraordinary case was disclosed at a meeting of the Chester Board of Guardians on Tuesday. The Clerk (Mr. Turnock) said that a person whom he described as Miss Hogg was admitted an inmate of the workhouse nine weeks ago. She was practically imbecile, and in hospital most of her time. A rumour reached him that she was by no means destitute, as the officials had been led to suppose, and he instituted investigations which ultimately resulted in the disclosure of the fact that Miss Hogg, who was being maintained out of the rates as a pauper, was worth no less than £7OO. She had two brothers, who said she was unmanageable at home, and they now proposed that she should remain in the work- house, they agreeing to pay 55. a week towards her maintenance.—Mr. Lee Okell : And they will look after the £7OO. (Laughter.) Councillor John Jones (the ex- sheriff of Chester) said the Board would not be justified in establishing a precedent by keeping in the workhouse as a pauper a person who had the means to maintain herself, and be well cared for outside. (Hear, hear.) He proposed that the brothers be requested to have her removed from the house.—This was seconded and agreed to.
At Wigston, noir Leicesser: on Wedne-dty, a large shoe factory was destroyed by fire) and 300 bands were thrown idle.

The work in connettfilon with the Ship Canal continnes to go on apace, and it is stated that the directors hope to be able to let in the water over the whole length by the end of next year. Many of the past difficulties of the company are attributable to the giving way of por- tions of the banks of the canal owing to the pressure of the moisture from adjoining land. In connection with this it may be stated that there is a considerable diffe- rence, from an engineering point of view, between the canal cutting and ordinary railway cuttings. In the for- mer case the cutting is considerably below the level of the sea, and consequently acts in the nature of a drain to the whole of the surrounding land. :illus- trative of this it may be stated that a large portion of a green field near Runcorn a short time ago forced itself sheer through a completed part of the embankment of the canal. The consequence was that many thousands of tons of earth bad to be simply replaced from whence it had been driven by the. moisture. Of course when the canal cutting is filled the water will act as a counterpoise, but until this stage is reached landslips may be almost daily expected. Another great difficulty that has to be contended with has been in connectim with the railway companies, who have so far persisted in exacting their pound of flesh to tha full extent. Where deviations have had to be constructed the railway engineers have seen with a vengeance that the work has been carried out in the best possible man- ner, and that the best snateriais have been used, with the result that the cost in this direction will be consider- ably snore than it would be under ordinary circum- stances. The railway companies, it is stated, in connection with these deviations also claim about a quarter of a million of money for extra haulage that may be involved, evidently everlooking the fact that on the other hand there must be a saving in the descent of those inclines if there are any. At present the Canal Company certainly don't look upon this appli- cation with a very favourable view, and no doubt more expense will be entailed in settling this difficulty. As a ray of hope to the anxious shareholders however, It has been pointed out that the estimated cost of the Suez Canal originally was about four millions, but before it was opened for traffic the cost had amounted to about fifteen millions. Notwithstanding this the £2O shares in that undertaking are now quoted at some- thing like £lOB to Llffil, and are practically unpurchase- able. There was also not the same engineering diffi- culties in the construction of the Suez Canal as in our own undertaking, and throughout its entire length not a lock had to be constructed. Further, it is the opinion of a gentleman preminently connected with the Board of Management, that when the Ship Canal is completed there will be a line of wharves extending from c.pd to end, which will of course considerably enhance the value of the shareholders' property. The land, also, which the company have been compelled to purchase, will, it is expected, realise an enormous profit, and already an offer has been refused for land situated on the banks of the canal on which it was proposed to erect a huge timber yard, owing to the disinclination of the directors at present to lay money out in preparing the required site. Taking these facts into consideration, therefore, it is to be hoped that shareholders will not quite give up , all hope of ever seeing any return for their money.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY IUGUST 13, 1802. - THE SHIP CANAL. THE LIMSING QUESTION AT WAR- RINGTON. A meeting of Warrington justices was hrld on Tuesday morning at the Court House for the pur- pose of appointing a licensing committee to deal with the basiness of the forthcoming brewsfer sessions for the borough. Alderman Holmes pre- sided, and there were about twelve magistrates present. The following gentlemen were appointed to form the licensing committee: Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Chandley,and Prancerab, Captain Ridgway and Messrs. F. Monks and J. Yairclough. These gentlemen also formed thern committee last year and the year previous, The ordinary brcwster sessions are to be held on the 23r1/ inst. and itlas been arranged that the applications for fresh licenses will be beard on the Zth„ There will this year be made the same applications for new licenses that have been made and rejected in previous years. Messrs. Greenali, Whitley, and Company will, for example, apply for a license to he granted to a new house to be erected at the coroner of Catherine-st., and Bewaey-road,and an application will also be raade for a license to be given to a house in the neighbourhood of Battersby-lane, and a full license will be asked for the "Grove," an offlslicensed house in F,ewsey-road. As we have said, all these appli- cations have been made before and refused, and it is hardly likely that the magistrates-will on this occasion reverse their previous decisions. In former years the Warrington Temperance Yedera- tiln have opposed the application, and it may be taken for granted that they will again be strenu- ously oppoz,ed this year. There are in the borough at present 87 houses occupied by licensed victual- lers, 48- occupied as beerhouses, and 70 off-licensed houses.

div.head: ST. HELENS BIGAMY CASE
div.p: THE ST. HELENS BIGAMY CASE

The magistrates at St. Helens Town Hall were I again occupied on Friday in connection with further proceedings arising out of the recent con- viction of James Harrison, of 2, Black Horse-st., Parr, of a charge of bigamy. llarrison surrendered himself to the police authorities for bigamy, and, subsequently, at Liverpool Assizes, was sentenced to three weeks' imprisonment. His wife instituted pro- ceedings for desertion, and the St. Helens Bench ordered him to contribute 10s. per week towards her support. On Thursday, Mary Ellen Wilson, with whom the defen- dant went through the form of marriage at Billinge, in 1887, summoned Harrison to show cause why he should not contribute to the Support of her two children. De- fendant, for whom Mr. J. O. Swift appeared, acknow- ledged that he was the father of the chifdren. Com- plainant gave formal evidence, after which Mr. Swift asked : I think that after you married him, and found out that he had a wife living, you left him 7—Complain- ant: Yes.—Mr. Swift remarked that a few weeks ago defendant was ordered to pay 10s, per week towards his wife's support. At that time he was getting 30s. per week, while now he was working as a labourer, and was only earning 18s. per week. Nothing had been paid under the order, and he (Mr. Swift had received instruc- tions to apply for a reduction of the order under the varied circumstances.—The Chairman: We shall want absolute proof of that.—Mr. Swift then called the de- fendant, who said that when he was at the police court a month ago he was earning 308. per week. He had, how- ever, injured himself internally, and could now only earn 18s. per week as a labourer.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay 24. ffd. per week for each child. At St. Helens, on Monday, Mr. J. 9. Swift, solicitor, applied on behalf of James Harrison, labourer, for the reduction of a magisterial order, under which he had to contribute 10s, per week towards the support of his wife, Mary Ellen. Mr. H. L. Riley appeared for the wife. —Mr. Swift stated that the magistrates had power to amend the order upon proof that the means of the hus- band or his wife had varied since the order was made. During the last month the applicant's means had con- siderably altered. He was formerly working as a sinker, and received 30s. and 328. per week, but he had received severe internal injury, and under the doctor's orders he had to discontinue his employment and obtain lighter work. This he was now doing and was in receipt of 18s. per week, out of which he was ordered fast Friday to pay ss. per week towards the support of his two chil- dren by the second woman, with whom he had gone through the form of marriage. He now made an offer to contribute 6s. per week towards his first wife's support. Mr. Riley, on behalf of the wife, agreed to accept the offer, remarking that he supposed the only alternative would be a refusal to pay anything. The Bench stated that the order would be reduced to 6s. per week.

div.head: STRANGE DEATH IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.
div.p: STRANGE DEATH IN RAINHILL ASYLUM.

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Rainhill Asylum, on Thursday morning, on the body of an inmate named George Potts, 35 years of age, a stableman, of Liverpool, who was formerly an in- mate of the Union Infirmary, West Derby, Liver- pool. The Coroner said on the 9th of this month he re- ceived from the asylum the ordinary statement giving notice of the death of George Potts. The authorities were bound to give him notice of alt deaths which took place in the asylum and annexe, whether from natural causes ot not. The cause of death was set out as general paralysis. • But afterwards the medical officers in the in- stitution made a post-mortem examination, as they did in a great many cases. When the post- mortem waS made it was found that Potts' eighth, ninth,' and tenth right and fifth and seventh left ribs were fractured. After this Dr. Menzies, the acting superintendent, in the absence of Dr. Wigles- worth, very properly wrote to him (the Coroner) giving him that information. The man had died in confine- ment, and it was their business to find out whether the ribs were fractured accidentally or otherwise. Dr. W. F. Menzies said the deceased was admitted into the asylum on the 6th May, 1891. He was not a man who had had any struggles with the attendants, and had no bruises of any sort. He had no suspicion during the man's lifetime that he suffered from fractured ribs. Dr. Walter Adam, assistant surgeon, said Potts was in the padded room from the night of the 29th June to the 4th August. While there he would sleep by himself. He was put into the padded room 'because.. he became ex- cited and restless, and was tearing his clothes. He knew nothing to lead him to believe that any of the attendants had done anything to the deceased. A paralytic's ribs were very triable, and a fall against a form or a table would easily break them. He imagined from what he saw of the ribs at the post- mortem examination that they had been broken several weeks. A Juror suggested that it was strange that Potts bad not complained of the pain, while another wondered how he could breathe with his ribs broken. Dr. Adam pointed out that general paralytics felt no pain, and Dr. Menzies subsequently explained that so long as there were one or two ribs to support the breast bone breath- ing was perfectly easy. Dr. E. T. Wynne, the patho- logist of the institution, who made the post-mortem ex- amination, said in his opinion the ribs had been frac- tured at least a month and not more than two months before death. The two attendants, Stanton and Gar- ner, said they knew nothing of the fracture. The latter intimated that on the 29th June he found Potts in his room in an excited state, perfectly naked, with all his clothes torn. The jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes, accelerated by fractured ribs, but how they were brought about there was no evi- dence to show. They did not attach any blame to the officials.

div.head: SPREAD OF CHOLERA.
div.p: THE SPREAD OF CHOLERA.
A CROWD FIRED INTO.

Advices received on Thursday at St. Petersburg state that cholera is declining. in the Caucasus and the Crimea, but spreading in the North of Russia. Twenty-three more Moscow factories have been closed. The latest daily cholera return issued at St. Petersburg shcws a great increase both in cases and deaths, the figures for the whole of Russia being 6,843 cases and 3,735 deaths. At Trebizonde, several hundreds of persons who are under- going quarantine revolted, and made an attemibt to break through the cordon. The local authorities sent for troops, who, after the crowd had been ordered to dis- perse, but refused, were ordered to fire. Seven of the crowd were killed and many wounded ,and the remainder retired in consternation to the lazaretto.
A Bombay telegram reports that another powerful trib- has joined the combination against the Ameer of Afghanistan.

div.head: MARRIAGE OF MM W. E. ATKIN.
div.p: MARRIAGE OF MM W. E. ATKIN.

On Thursday the marriage was celebrated at Dunstablie, Bedfnrdshire, of Mr. William Ernest Atkin, of "' Middilhurst " House, Grappenhall, the popular secretary of the Warrington Musical Society, and manager for the Tanners Lane Tanning Co., Warrington, to Miss Mein, second daughter of Mrs. Mein of the Manor House, Dunstable. The ceremony was performed at the parish church by the Rev. Canon Macaulay, the vicar, the. best man being Mr. Crosland Grahame, of Lancashire. Th•e bride wore a white silk dress, covered with old lace, and a pearl necklace, and Lad the usual wreath of orange blossoms, and fall, and she carried a beautiful shower bouquet of white flOwers. The bridesmaids were Miss Jane Mein, Miss- Carrie Mein, Miss Emmie Mein, sisters of the bride,. Miss Gert- rude Atkin, sister of the bridegroom, and Miss Marah Robinson, cousin of the bride. They were attired in dresses of yellow silk, trimmed with white, and Leghorn hats to match, trimmed with flowers, and they carried shower boquets composed of green and yellow flowers to match their hats. The congregation was very large and included Mrs. Atkin, mother of the bridgegroom, Mr. R. W. Row- son, cousin of the bridegroom; and M. Frank H.. Crossley, conductor of the. Warrington Musical Society. There was an "at home "at the residence of the bride's mother in the afternoon, after which the pair took their departure for Oxfordrthenee to proceed to Devonshire. The wedding presents numbered about 160 to 170, and comprised some most handsome and costly articles.

div.head: BREACHES OF THE FACTO4tY ACTS_
div.p: BREACHES OF THE FACTO4tY ACTS_

At the Warrington borough magistrates" court, yesterday, before Mr. John White (chairman), and Alderman Harrison, the Burton Cycle C 0.,. Beweey- mt., were charged by C. W. Shaw, lI.Mi inspector of factories, that they did on the 28th of May, that being a Saturday, employ Edward Ash brook, a per- son under 14 years of age, atter two o'Clock in. the , afternoon. The Inspector said there had, been no, previous conviction, and he would not press for a. , heavy penalty.—Mr. Burton said the lad was merely being employed in the stores that•afternoon,. and happened to be passing through the store room when a man who was repairing a bicycle asked him to give him a hand, and he did so I without his, Mr. Burton's, knowledge. The day I was their stock-taking day.—The defendants were let off with payment of costs, 75., without fa conviction— Mary Ann Brown, dress-maker, Bridge Street, was • charged by the factory Inspector, with employing two persons, Clara Turner and Florence Smith, after 4- o'clock on Saturday, May 28th.—Mr. Johnson,.sub- inspector said he visited the defendant's premises at 28' minutes to son the afternoon of the date men- tioned and found the girls mentioned at work.— The defendant's father appeared to represent her. He said this was an exceptional case, in which a girl had been away all that week, and another stopped away on the Saturday, and the work was really required to be sent in by 4- o'clock, and it threw them behind. The girls, were not of the ages stated. Turner was 19 and the other girl 18. The defendant was not in the htbit of doing tnis kind of thing, and the girls did not start till half past 8' in the morning, though the defendant was entitled to start them at B.—The Inspector said they could be worked till 10 p.m. 48 days in the year any day except Saturday.—The defendant's father promised that the offence should not occur again, and she was fined in. thelowest penalty, of is. and costs.

div.head: CROFT.
div.p: CROFT.

A WONDERFUL CHERRY TREE.—A correspondent writes: lam informed that Mr. John Green, near St. Lewis' Roman Catholic Chapel, Croft, has a cherry tree. which, is now bearing fruit for the second time this season. The tree, which had previously a fair crop of full-grown cherries on, is now bearing cherries of smaller degree, and of a much darker colour. The cherries are, however, very sweet and good.

tioirricurzunar, SOCISTY.—The gardens entered for competition for the prizes offered by the above society, for the neatest and best cultivated cottagegardens,were judged on Saturday afternoon, by Mr. IL Harrison, of Newton, the appointed judge, who was accompaniea to, the gardens by Mr. W. Fazakerley, one of the members of the committee,though he took no part in the judging. The [Lumber of gardens entered for competition was eight, but one, however, was withdrawn. The awards. will be made known at the society's annual show. The whole of the gardens presented a very satisfactory appearance.

Picncs.—A few picnic parties came to the village on Saturday and Sunday. On Saturday a picnic parry numbering 50 persons was conveyed from, the Joiners Arm Hotel, Croft, in two large wagonettes to Southport.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

ASIZEP IN CHARGE OF A HORSH AND WlnoN.—At the Alirinchain Petty Sessions, on Monday, Win. Shuffre- bottom, aged 21, a carter in the employ of Mr. John Blackledge, of Lymm, was summoned for being asleep while in charge of a horse and wagon while going through Altrincham on July 16th.—Defendant pleaded guilty, and said he had been to Manchester with, some farm produce, and on coming home he had just dropped asleep when the offioer came up.—The Bench fined the defendant ss. including costs, and the same time re- marking on the danger of people going to, sleep while in charge of conveyances.

RiSHIIEkRING.—As this village festival appears to wane in the estimation of the residents, the interested outsider takes it up with redoubled energy. Since the Local Board set its foot down agaihst the Cross and village being turned into a fair ground the popularity of the rushbearing has gradually been on the wane. 'The great competitors of the fair are undoubtedly the cheap excursions which tempt people out of; the village on Monday, the chief day of the carnival.. Trips to South- port, Liverpool, Belle Vue, /cc., will each, have their patrons, and on Tuesday . morning, people begin to settle down to work during the day,, but at night the show comes in for a fair sprinkling of customers. The morris dancers are coming out on Saturday morning in their usual gay costumes, and no one will have reason to complain that the " pan" has not been poked at them.

div.head: NEW CONVENT AT BLACEBROOK,
div.p: NEW CONVENT AT BLACEBROOK,
NEAR ST. HELENS.

The St. Helens Corporation have passed plans for a new convent at Blackbrook. About twenty-live years ago the Sisters of Mercy, of Mount Vernon-st. Convent, Liverpool, were requested by the late Bishop Goss to establish a branch honse at Black- brook, and at his request Blaekbrook House was given to them at a mere nominal rent. The rates, however, together with the constantly increasing ex- penses for repairs and general maintenance, made the place far too costly for the nuns. Moreover, the house was much too large, as well as otherwise unsuited, for a small community, and for those reasons the nuns recently decided to leave it. The news of the decision was painful in the extreme to the people of Blackbrook, where their devoted care of the school children and their constant readiness to visit the sick or to relieve the distressed, irrespective of creed, have naturally pro- cured for the nuns a high place in the people's esteem, and a strong hold upon their affection. The matter was ' at once taken up by the congregation. They saw imme- diately that it was for their advantage in every way to retain the nuns' services, and they unanimously agreed to provide them with a suitable residence. The building has, in fact, been already begun, the plans having been executed by Mr. P. Ball, Messrs. J. and J. Almond, St. Helens, being the builders. The cost is estimatad to reach about 23 per family in St. Mary's congregation; but as the cost of their new infant school must also be provided by them they expect help from some of the St. Helens shopkeepers, with whom most of the money from Haydock, Blackbrook, and Parr, is spent, and also from some of the local labour employers, for whose works the children are being carefully trained. It may be added that nearly 400 children attend the Blackbrook day schools, ever fifty of them being non-Catholics, and that at their last examination the three departments—boys, girls, and infants—which are all taught by the nuns, got the highest merit mark, viz., "Excellent," from her Majesty's inspector I:eraeculas,,s,ad.gfe,w---- the diocese= gifts and sonptuial, kuowtedge. , in.specter for religious

div.head: WAS, SIIIILLEY AN ATHEIST?
div.p: WAS, SIIIILLEY AN ATHEIST?

In connection with the recent Shelley Centenary, the Rev. Frank IL. Treeston preached on the above subject in Cairo-st. Chapel, on Sunday morning. Taking as text the words of St. Paul "As certain even of your own poete have said," he remarked that England hadjust been paying centennial honour to th,i memory of one of her own poets. No such honour, however, was paid to him during life.. On the contrary, he was expelled from his collbge in Oxford, then driven from his father's door, after- wards deprived of his-own children, and by nearly everybody denounced as a confessed and convicted atheist. But was Shelley an atheist? Common opinion considered he was, and still branded him with the-name. Now that his fame was again, to the front, it would bewell,.however, to examine the charge : if true, to admit it, if false, to refute it. The preacher then pointed out that the charge chiefly rested on three small pamphlets, viz., The Necessity of Atheism; it kflatatiotv of Deism, and An Essay on Christianity,. and proceeded to deal with these writings in detail. He showed that the first was little more than an undergraduate's thesis,, prompted by a fearless search for intellectual truth,. and maintained that it ought to have been answered instead of punished by the extreme and unjust penalty of summary expulsion. By this ill-treat— ment Shelley was inevitably driven into revolt against current religion and orthodox Christ- ianity. The one apppeared mere convention„ and the other empty tradition. But, as the preacher next proved by quotations from his other writings, Shelley.' S real opposition was not against religion itself, nor yet indeed against Christ s Christianity. ttis atheism, so-called, was not a blank and blatant denial of every idea of deity. He dis- believed, no doubt, in the artibrary deity of orthodox theology, but he believed in a universal spirit pervading-and overruling the-world. He was not an atheist, but a pantheist. He was not a Christian according to the doctrinal tests which so many good people delight to, set um but he had a deep veneration for Christ himself,.he spoke of him as, "that sublime humadcharacter,"'ana he pleaded that the spirit of Christ should more and more actu- ate all human life. What he denounced and discarded was not God,but the crude idea ef God put forward in his day, not Christ but the dogmatic theory of Christ which usurped the place of Christ himself. In conclusion Mr. Freeston said he rejeiced at this opportunity of defending the name of Shelley from unjust misconception. Because the young poet had the courage to put truth higher than creed, he thereby drew down upon him the opposition of orthodox religion and paid a. bitter penalty. But he implored them always to refuse to identify religion with orthodoxy, or Christianity uith dogmatic theology. Ile was anxious that they should be free from the guilt of . passing a heedless and unjust verdict. Shelley made mistakes in life, which no one could wish to defend, but he had a high ideal of truth, he loved liberty, he hated bigotry, he worked for humanity, and he reverenced deity.

CEMETERY.
A STRANGE CUSTOM OF SHOEMAKER& "SCENE" AT THE POIiICE COURT.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yester- day, William Allen,of Manchester-lane,.was charged with using threatening language to Frederick Arthur Essenhigh, monumental' sculptor;. 130, Bat- tersby-lane, on Thursday week; in. the Cemetery.— Mr. Longton appeared for the pnosecution,. and Air. P. Davies for the defence.—Mr. Langton said Allen had been in the employ of the complainant when he was in partnership with his, brother and the firm was Essenhigh Bros. Allen. was discharged twelve months ago,.and since then he had taken- it into his head to be dangerously annoying to his former master, who was the one of the firm who discharged him. On Thursday week about threco'clock. the com- plainant was pursuing his business in the cemetery, when Allen came in and used very abusive and threat- ening languar. Mr. Essenhigh remonstrated with him, and told him if he would not leave him alone he would have to summon him. Allen put hiafist in Essenhigh's face and threatened to strike him, and said he would punch him out of the place. Mr. Essenhigh was unable to continue his own business on account of the defend- ant's threats 'and conduct.—Alderman Hedrrison : Where was the registrar of the cemetery that he permitted this shameful conduct to go on ? Mr: Essenhigh and others corroborated Mr. hongton's statement, and it appeared! that Allen previously had a pair of boots , repaired by Mr. Frank Dunn,. and witness had these I boots sent to him and -tried tem on. He knew they were Allen's boots. They did not fit him, and he gave I them to a man named John Shaw in payment of wages. The defendant in the 'Cemetery asked him about he boots and he referred him to Mr. Dunn It seemed that Allen did not call for his boots at Dunn's, and was not in the town, and Dunn could not learn where he was, therefore, according to the- custom of the trade in such cases,sold them to Mr. Essenhigh for the cost of repairs. —Mr. Davies commented strongly on this custom as illegal,. and it was stated in said he envoidtencaweartehattharsst eitnhwigahs bought the boots, thinking Allen was not coming back for them. Allen was away for seven weeks at Thal- wall, and it was during that time the boots were sold. Essenhigh said he discharged Allen for using abusive lan- guage, but there waS a counter statement that Allen left because he would not work for such a man as Essenhigh. In the course of the prooeelngs, Mr. Davies remarked as to Allen being alleged to have threatened to knock Essenhigh's head off if he would go under some trees that had it been his (Mr. Davies's) case lie would have knocked his head off.—Alderman Harrison: There's no account- ing for tastes.—Later an Mr. Langton happened to drop a remark while Mr. Davies was on his feet, when the Latter between whom and the former there had been some friction during the morning, exclaimed " I wish you would be quiet. I never saw such an impertinent:puppy. —Alderman llarrison (angrily) : We won't have this court turned into a bear garden. You have no right to use such language to any professional gentleman, and I won't sit here to hear it.—Mr. Davies : lam very sorry. —Alderman Harrison: So am L—Mr. Davies: Am I the only one who uses improper language in this court ? Will you allow me to conduct the case without interfering with me. I am going to conduct it, and no one else.---Aldermin Harrison : I will not have my ears polluted like that by a professional gentleman.—Mr. Davies Polluted !—Alderman Harri- . .

;on : You called Mr. Longton an impudent puppy.—Mr. Davies : I did not call him an impudent puppy. I said impertinent puppy.—The Chairman: I will stop the case if this sort of thing goes on.—After some evidence for the defence, the Bench bound Allen over in his own recognisances of £5 to keep the peace for 6 months, and ordered him to pay costs, the Chairman remarking that though they were not quite sure as to Essenhigh's con. duct about the boots, yet Allen had no right to go and threaten him in that manner.
AN UNPOPULAR REPRIEVE.

A Tennessean lawyer Who had murdered a brother practitioner in a most deliberate manner was sentenced to death a long time ago. He carried his case before num- berless courts, but in each his sentence was confirmed, and it will therefore be understood that his crime was of a peculiarly heinous character. On the eve of his execution, however, he was reprieved by Mr. Buchnan , the govenor of the States This remarkable instance of clemency has produced an explosion of rage in Memphis and the Governor has been hanged in effigy by a crowd of citizens, who would also have lynched the murderer if he had not been removed. The Governor, however, can afford to disregard such manifestations. He has no doubt, solid and convincing reasons, Whit interposition.

It is interesting to note that Mr. Gladstone and Mr. Villa's both of whom took part in rhursday night's division—Mr. Gladstone for the amendment and Mr. Villers against—voted on opposite sides in the division of January, 1835. when Sir Charles Manners Sutton .after- wards Lord Canterbury, was ejected from the chair by the Whigs. The positions are,however, now reversed,for in 1835 Mr. Glad stone was in the•minority and Mr. Villers in the majority.
THE QUEEN AND MR. GLADSTONE:
TIM MANDATE
TO FORM A GOVERNMENT.

Sir Henry Ponsonby called on Mr. Gladstone yesterday and as a result it is understood that Mr. Gladstone's presence at Osborne will not be necessary until early next week, when he will practically have formed his Cabinet and can personally submit the names to her Majesty for approval and sanction. Mr. Hibbert, M.P., and Mr. Arnold Morley, have been in conference for some time this afternoon with Mr. Gladstone. THE GROUSE SEASON.,

The 15th opene d in the North of Scotland yesterday morning in dull th ough pleasant weather,' but owing to the sitting of Parliament many shooting lodges are as yet unoccupied. There is a good average stook of birds on the higher grounds, kit on lower grounds they are scarce and wild. Birds are also plentiful in Reafrew- shire, Dambartonshire, and Stirlingshire, and a great number of shooting parties • are out in Annandale. There is little sport, owing to the prevalence of a dense mist. TFIE OUTGOING AND INCOMING PREMIERS.

After Lord Salisbury's departure for Osborne, the Hon. Schomberg M'Donnell called at Carlton-gardens, and had an interview with Mr. Gladstone's private secretary. It is understood that communicationd have passed between the Privy Council and Mt. Gladstone this morning relative to the date when he wouldlbe pre- pared to order a meeting next week of the Council for the change of Seals. The function, it is belitmed, will not take, place until Wednesday. This will,. however, be in time to enable writs to be moved for in the house on Thursday for those members who accept office in the new Administration.

div.head: POLITICAL SITUATIONS
div.p: ThE POLITICAL SITUATIONS
FINAL ARRANGEMENTS FOR RES/GNING. DEPARTURE OF LORD SALISBURY FOR OSBORNE.

The lest Cabinet Council under Lord Salisbury's Government met at 12.15 p.m. yesterday at the Foreign-office, Lord Salisbury presiding, when final arrangements were made for resigning ales-. Dur- ing the past week the Government offutials have been exceedingly busy closing up their work, and the Ministers have nearly all made.the necessary , preparations for leaving their offices, se that only one or two would remain in town after yesterday. The meeting was a very short one, and Itcoke up before one o'clock, when uaost of ths Ministers bade each other good-bye as they left the Foreign- office. MR. GLADSTONE AND HIS SUPPORXERS.

Mr. Gladstone rose early yesterday morning, and at eleven o'clock went for a drive in an open victoria, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone. Mr. Gladstone on returning to Carlton.gardens from his drive received several visitors. Mr. Arnold Morley called shortly after noon and remained for some time with the right hon. gentleman. Lord Herschell and Professor Stuart also had interviews with Mr. Gladstone.

div.head: REMARKABLE .DIVIBION..
div.p: A REMARKABLE .DIVIBION..

The division on Mr. Asquith's amendment on Thursday night (the " Morning Post "states) was in so.me respects the most remarkable that has ever taking place in living memory. Every member of the house, except one who is in Australia, either voted or paired, and the total number of absentees was only, three,. vizt, Mr. Curran, and Messrs. Wharton and Winterbotham, the two last- named being away through illness. Six hundred and sixty members voted, so that, iucluding the Speaker and four tellers, 665 were present. The three absentees above named and the vacant seats of. Northeast Cork and Holborn account for the total ,membership of 670. Mr. Cremer, notwithstanding severe illness, eame down to record his vote, add was supported from the lobby into the house by two fellow members. the nearest approach to this division was that taken on the second reading of the House Rule Bill of 1886; when, including the Speaker and the tellers, 657 members were present and only 13 absent, Several hon. gentlemen travelled, tong distances to take part in the division. a notable ease being that of Mr. Ernest Spencer, who had to excuse himself from dining with the King of the Belgians at Ostend in order to record his vote. Reckoning Mr. Goschen and Mr. Carson as Liberal. Unionists, the figures were :—Conservatives, 263 Liberal Unionists, 47 ; total 3ICI. Gladstonians, 2714. Anti-Parnellites, 7; Parnellites 9 ; total, 350. The other members present were the tellers—Mr. Akers- Douglas and Sir W. Walrond (Conservative) and Mr. Asquith and Mr. Burt (Gladstonian)—and the Speaker. DEPARTURE OF LORD SALISBURY FOR OSBORN'S,. Lord Salisbury left Victoria Station by special train,. at five o'clock for Osborne. to deliver into her Majesty'S hands the formal resignation of the Government. His lordship was attended to the station by the Hon. ISchomberg M'Donnell. Lord Salisbury remained at 1 Osborne last night as the guest of the Queen, and will return to town to-day.

Messrs. Charles Caramel' and Co., of Workington, have entered into negotiations with the directors of the West Cumberland orks for the purchase of the blast furnaces and also for the whole of the punt ii these steel works. The furnaces, which are sin i,, number, tc- gether with those of the Derwent Woi as, will be kept going for the manufacture of pig irNi tor the use of the Workington Steel Works and thp Cyclops Works t Sheffield. In the event of the punhase being effected it is probable that the West Cumber?and Steel Works will be entirely reconstructed, and adapted for plate mills and other manufactures in the steel trade. It is under- stood that if the purchase is satisfactorily complded arrangements will be made for a long lease of the ground. The West Cumberland Works, which foruerly employed 2,000 men, are now idle. ,

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. DANCING, SINGING, AND MUSIC LICENSES. The Public Health Acts Amendment Act, 1890. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that Applications for Licenses for places used for public dancing, singing, music, or other public entertainment of the like kind, must be made to the Licensing justices at their General Annual Licensing meeting, or at any adjournment thereof. Fourteen days' previous notice of the intention to apply for any such license must be given to the Clerk of the Justices and to the Chief Constable. Any person who keeps any house, room, garden, or other place (whether licensed or not for the sale of wine, s9irits, or beer) for dancing, singing, music, or other public enter- tainment of the like kind without a license for that purpose. will be deemed guilty of keeping a disorderly house, and liable to a penalty not exceeding .R 5 for every day during which the offence continue,. Dated this Bth day of August, 1892. J. LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk. COUNTY OF CHESTER. NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that at the General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, holden at Chester Castle, in and for the County of Chester, on the 27th day of June, 1892. IT WAS ORDERED, pursuant to the provisions of "The Licensing Acts, 1872-1874," that the Meetings of the County Licensing Committee relative to the confirm- ation of New Licenses be held as follows : viz. :—The Meeting of the Chester Licensing Committee on SATUR- DAY, the Ist day of October next, at Chester Castle, at One o'clock in the afternoon; and a the Knutsford Licensing Committee at the Court House, Nether, Knutsford, on MONDAY, the 3rd day of October next, at Two o'clock in the afternoon. And Notice is Hereby also Given, that the said Meet- ings on the Ist and 3rd of October respectively will be especially convened under the provision in that behalf contained in the 32nd section of " The Licensing Act, 1874," for the purpose of making (if deemed necessary) orders under that section with respect to towns and populous places. By the Court, REGINALD POTTS, Clerk of the Peace for the said County. 9th August, 1892. NOTE.—By the Rules applicable to the said Meetings it is directed that "Any person applying for the confirmation of a grant "of a new License by the Licensing Justices shall give "Notice to the Clerk of the Peace of such application, "two days before the meeting of the Committee, within "the district to which tile house in respect of which the "License has been granted is situate. "In case any person shall appear, either by himself, "his counsel, or attorney, before the Licensing Justices "and oppose the grant of a new License, he shall be at "Liberty so to appear either by himself, his counsel, or. "attorney, before the Licensing Committee for the "district, and oppose the confirmation of the grant of "such new License, upon giving to the applicant and to "the Clerk of the Peace notice in writing of his inten- " tion so to do not less than two days before the meeting "of such committee, and "All appli,ations for the addition to Towns adjacent "Collections of Houses, or for Declarations of Areas to "be Populous Places under the 32nd Section of the Act "of 1874, must, in every instance, be accompanied by a "plan of the proposed addition or area (as the case may "be), which plan must, previously to the meeting of "the Licensing Committee, have been submitted to the "Magistrates sitting in Petty Sessions for the Division "within which the proposed addition or area shall be "situate, in order that such Magistrates may express "their opinion thereon for the information of the "Licensing Committees."
